div.p: Myne het 'n vasgestelde lewensduur, wat beteken dat hul sluiting onvermydelik is. Navorsing dui egter histories daarop dat mynmaatskappye nie hul bedrywighede met sluiting in gedagte beplan nie.

Dit word ondersteun deur die feit dat mynsluiting-en rehabilitasiestrategieë in Suid-Afrika tot dusver nie baie suksesvol was nie, wat tot duisende verlate myne regoor die land gelei het. Die onsuksesvolle sluiting van myne handhaaf sosiaal-ekologiese kwesbaarheid in omliggende gemeenskappe, veral teen die impakte van klimaatsverandering. Mynsluiting bied 'n geleentheid om die sosiaal-ekologiese veerkragtigheid van die omliggende gemeenskap teen geprojekteerde impakte op klimaatsverandering te verhoog, ná 'n myn se leeftydperk. Alhoewel daar baie literatuur oor die geprojekteerde impakte van klimaatsverandering in Suid-Afrika is, is studies wat die mate waartoe mynsluiting-en rehabilitasiestrategieë klimaatsveranderingoorwegings insluit, ondersoek beperk.
Die doel van hierdie navorsing is om hierdie leemte in die literatuur aan te spreek.

Deur 'n kwalitatiewe benadering te gebruik, ondersoek hierdie studie hoe mynmaatskappye in Suid-Afrika die sosiaal-ekologiese veerkragtigheid van omliggende gemeenskappe teen klimaatsverandering se impakte kan versterk deur klimaatsveranderingaanpassing in mynsluiting-en rehabilitasiestrategieë aan te neem. Data is uit semi-gestruktureerde onderhoude met myndeskundiges, vanuit beleidsomvangbepaling, en uit 'n gestruktureerde oorsig van mynmaatskappye se jaarlikse en volhoubaarheidsverslae ingesamel. Hierdie navorsing se bevindinge beklemtoon drie hoofaspekte vir die aanvaarding van klimaatsveranderingaanpassing in mynsluitingen rehabilitasiestrategieë: (1) riglyne van beste praktyk het 'n aansienlike invloed op mynsluiting-en rehabilitasieaktiwiteite; (2) die Suid-Afrikaanse regulasies wat mynsluiting reguleer, speel 'n deurslaggewende rol in die leiding van die verandering wat in die industrie benodig word; en (3) die mynbedryf moet 'n toenemende fokus op die waarde van belanghebbendes se betrokkenheid plaas tydens die beplanning vir sluiting en rehabilitasie.

Hierdie tesis assesseer ook die voordele en uitdagings daarvan om klimaatsveranderingaanpassing in mynsluiting-en rehabilitasiestrategieë te inkorporeer. Bevindinge beklemtoon hoe die toename in geïntegreerde mynsluiting en progressiewe rehabilitasie vroeë aanduidings van suksesvolle en volhoubare mynsluiting in Suid-Afrika, en wêreldwyd, verskaf. Laastens word die insigte vanuit hierdie navorsing gebruik om praktiese aanbevelings te ontwikkel om mynmaatskappye te help om reaksies op klimaatsaanpassing as deel van hul sluitings-en rehabilitasiestrategieë aan te neem en te implementeer, asook om alternatiewe oplossings tot klimaatsaanpassing voor te stel wat op natuurgebaseerde oplossings en ekosisteem-gebaseerde aanpassings fokus.

More importantly, however, this study focuses on mine closure in South Africa due to the country's long history of mine abandonment and failed closure, with many more mines projected to close in the coming decade as the country shifts away from coal and many mines near their operational end-of-life (Crous, 2020). Evidence suggests that South Africa is littered to date with thousands of abandoned mines, waste dumps, quarries and other sites (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Edwards & Maritz, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020), posing both environmental and social threats. For these reasons, it is particularly important to understand current closure practices in South Africa and identify opportunities for improvement to achieve sustainable and effective transitions post-closure.

div.head: List of Tables
div.p: Environmental and social threats associated with the mining industry may also be exacerbated by climate change impacts, which are expected to become significantly worse in the next few years, posing a significant threat for mine closure.

South Africa is already experiencing climate change impacts, including rising temperatures and an increase in the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall events (Ripple et al., 2022). South Africa is also particularly vulnerable to climate change, as impacts are argued to exacerbate existing vulnerabilities, such as low employment rates and high levels of poverty (Szabo et al., 2016). As such, poor and informal communities in South Africa are increasingly vulnerable to climate change impacts, due to existing sensitivities and a lack of adaptive capacity to climatic shocks such as flash flooding, droughts, and heat waves (Hlahla & Hill, 2018). Importantly, mining communities could be considered particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts when the mine reaches operational closure and beyond, due to the social and economic circumstances of these communities.

Currently, a lot of the focus in the literature is on climate change adaptation and reducing the vulnerability of the urban poor to climate change impacts in South Africa (Bai et al., 2018). However, significantly less attention has been paid to reducing vulnerability in rural communities, particularly in mining communities, to projected climate change impacts. Mining communities have similar socio-economic challenges to the urban poor in South Africa (Rankoana, 2020), but with the added risk of being dependent on the mine which carries significant implications after closure. Whilst not always the case, some communities surrounding mines in South Africa face high levels of job dependency or unemployment, low levels of education, informality, and poor or inadequate service delivery, which make them more vulnerable and exposed to climate change impacts as a result, particularly once the mine has ceased operations (Cole & Broadhurst, 2020). In the context of this research a mining community is defined as a geographical area or locality where the lives and livelihoods of its residents are significantly influenced, if not dominated, by the presence and activities of mining operations (Cole and Broadhurst, 2020). Often, these types of communities include individuals and families whose economic well-being is directly linked to the mining industry, either through employment in the mines or related industries, such as mining services or supply chains (Cole and Broadhurst, 2020). In addition to economic ties, a mining community often experiences social, environmental, and infrastructure impacts associated with mining activities (Rankoana, 2020).

These can include housing provided by mining companies, social services, and infrastructure development, but also challenges such as environmental degradation, health and safety concerns, and social disruptions (Cole and Broadhurst, 2021).

With South Africa experiencing the tangible consequences of climate change impacts, particularly amongst more vulnerable communities, an urgent need arises for the integration of climate change adaptation measures across multiple sectors. div.head: Problem Statement
div.p: Existing social-ecological vulnerabilities within mining communities in South Africa make these communities particularly sensitive to projected climate change impacts, particularly once the mine ceases operations and no longer provides residents with financial, social, and economic support. The fact that mines have a set lifespan means that their eventual closure is inevitable. Therefore, it is crucial to ensure that the communities that rely on and live near the mine whilst it is active can continue to live a sustainable life once the mine closes. Social vulnerabilities characteristic of these communities are heightened post-closure, and therefore, any additional stresses (such as those caused by climate change) have a more significant negative impact on mining communities.

Currently, evidence suggests that mine closure and rehabilitation strategies have not been very successful in South Africa, resulting in thousands of abandoned and unsuccessfully closed mines across the country (Watson & Olalde, 2019). Unsuccessful mine closure and mine abandonment perpetuate social-ecological vulnerability within surrounding communities, particularly to climate change impacts such as flash flooding, water scarcity, and prolonged drought events. Mine abandonment and unsuccessful closure are related concepts in the context of mining, but they differ in their nature and implications (Mpanza et al., 2021). Mine abandonment refers to the decision to stop active mining operations, while unsuccessful closure reflects the challenges and problems that arise when mining operations are concluded in a manner that does not adequately address long-term environmental, social, and economic impacts (Mpanza et al., 2021). An abandoned mine can be successfully closed with proper planning and management, but an unsuccessful closure often signifies a lack of effective post-mining measures (van Druten & Bekker, 2017). However, it is important to highlight that both unsuccessful mine closure and mine abandonment can lead to negative social and environmental consequences (Watson & Olalde, 2019).

Although there is a lot of literature on projected climate change impacts in South Africa, building social-ecological resilience, and restoring ecosystems, there are limited studies exploring the extent to which mine closure and rehabilitation strategies incorporate climate change considerations and social-ecological resilience. Mine closure plans present an opportunity to increase the socialecological resilience of the surrounding community to projected climate change impacts, beyond the mine's operational phase.

div.head: Research Objectives
div.p: The aim of this research is to explore the potential to strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mining communities in the face of climate change impacts by incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa. As such, the research objectives are as follows:
• Identify examples of mine closure strategies and projects in South Africa that already incorporate climate change adaptation thinking.

• Determine the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure plans in South Africa, for both the mining company and the surrounding community and environment.

• Evaluate the extent to which incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa can strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts.

div.head: Research Approach
div.p: Unlike a quantitative research approach, qualitative research is exploratory and can be used when the researcher does not have a clear idea of the findings of the research. As such, my research objectives were aimed at unearthing deeper meaning and understanding (Preiser et al., 2022) of my research topic. Adopting this research approach allowed me to enhance my comprehension of intricate concepts, social dynamics, and cultural occurrences, as highlighted in the interview discussions (Bryman et al., 2019). The chosen research approach was consistent with my objective of delving deeply into the distinctive viewpoints of a specific subset of participants. These perspectives helped shed light on climate change adaptation within the framework of mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa.

In line with my intentions to gain a better understanding of the complexities, nuances, and interdependencies inherent in mining companies and surrounding social-ecological systems, as well as the impacts of climate change on this complex system, I adopted a constructivist and interpretivist ontological stance and subjective epistemological paradigm. In line with Charmaz's perspective (2005), as researchers, we actively participate in the construction and interpretation of qualitative data. In other words, our findings are often reflective of our interpretation rather than completely objective. As such, whilst constructivism is a useful overarching paradigm, I also incorporated an interpretivist paradigm in this research process to focus on the meanings, experiences, and interpretations that the specialists divulged during the interview process. This approach was complemented by an inductive analysis of the data collected to capture the complexity of socialecological systems and the interconnected nature of mining companies.

Given the limitations associated with individual research methods for understanding social-ecological systems (de Vos et al., 2022), I collected data from several different sources and employed multiple data collection methods throughout this research process, to enhance the credibility and validity of my findings. Multi-method approaches are becoming increasingly popular, particularly when considering the complexities associated with social-ecological systems (de Vos et al., 2022), making a multi-method approach useful for understanding the complexities associated with the socialecological resilience of mines in South Africa. I collected data via a combination of report reviews, policy scoping, and semi-structured interviews. I also conducted a literature review to establish the contextual background for my study.

div.head: Significance of the Study
div.p: Through this research, I aim to contribute to the increased recognition of climate change adaptation's role in strengthening social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts, particularly for communities post mine closure. Furthermore, the outcomes could serve as valuable insights to guide additional empirical research endeavors and lay the groundwork for suggesting further study recommendations.

This study could prove valuable for mining companies seeking to integrate climate change adaptation within their mine closure and rehabilitation strategies, with the aim of enhancing the social-ecological resilience of communities impacted by the cessation of mining operations. The results offer a potential roadmap for embracing climate change adaptation measures, including approaches like nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based adaptation, within closure and rehabilitation strategies.
This can hopefully serve the best interests of all stakeholders post-closure.

Importantly, the conclusions I have drawn endorse the ongoing partnership between mining companies, the South African government, and impacted communities, aiming for systemic transformation, regardless of the scale of achievable results. It is foreseeable that the practical insights derived from my findings could be instrumental in pinpointing potential hurdles obstructing change initiatives and driving effective, sustainable closure.

Given the global presence of mining and the predicted increase in mine closures in the coming decade, this study may be of significance beyond South Africa's borders, particularly in more vulnerable mining areas. By highlighting the insufficient attention given to crucial aspects such as rehabilitation, successful closure, and community development, the study's findings offer valuable insights into the local mining industry, which may be of relevance to the global mining industry. Furthermore, the study's exploration of the challenges in integrating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies could contribute to a broader understanding of the complexities involved.

This understanding, in turn, might aid governments and policy-makers in formulating effective policies and legislation that incentivize and enable the seamless integration of climate change adaptation measures into mine closure processes. This study, therefore, has the potential to catalyze positive changes in how mining companies worldwide approach sustainability and environmental responsibility in order to achieve long-term, sustainable closure that benefits all stakeholders.

div.head: Mine Closure and Rehabilitation
div.p: Mine closure planning is a well-established practice and a vital element of a mine's life cycle (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016). As such, the planning for mine closure is an important component spanning the entire lifecycle of a mine, commencing with project design and assessment for mining approval, extending through commissioning, operations, decommissioning, and culminating in final closure and rehabilitation (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016;Watson and Olalde 2019). In other words, mine closure planning should be an iterative, proactive process that expands, adjusts, and becomes more detailed as end-of-life approaches. This enhances the efficacy of mine closure plans and ensures that all possible outcomes have been thought of and included (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016). It is important to note that mine closure goes beyond environmental restoration and should also encompass the rebuilding of the surrounding community to be effective (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016). Ultimately, an effective mine closure plan should enable communities to achieve an improved, or sustained, quality of life beyond life of mine (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016;Sesele et al., 2021).

Mine closure and rehabilitation refer to two separate processes, which can either happen simultaneously or at varying times during the life cycle of a mine. Mine closure refers to the activities conducted when a mine's operational phase concludes, or has already concluded, and the process of final decommissioning and mine rehabilitation is initiated (Grant et al., 2016). Conversely, mine rehabilitation involves the process of restoring the landscape after mining to achieve the intended post-mining land use (Grant et al., 2016). The activities that occur at a mine site after operations have ceased are ultimately what defines the long-term impact on the area's social, economic, environmental, and institutional development (Grant et al., 2016). As such, an integrated mine closure approach should consider social, environmental, and economic factors from the early stages of the mine and continue to do so throughout operations (Grant et al., 2016;ICMM, 2019). Critical to the integrated mine closure process is the need to consider closure as a fundamental element of the mine's core business (Morrison-Saunders et al. 2016;Watson and Olalde 2019;Grant et al. 2016).

In order to address the adverse effects linked with mining operations and to secure favorable outcomes for local communities, mining companies are obligated to achieve thorough and effective rehabilitation of mining sites (Manero et al., 2020). For sites that have been fundamentally altered by mining activities, it is impractical to restore the land to pre-mining conditions or for the complete restoration of historical ecosystems (Doley & Audet, 2013). In these instances, Doley and Audet (2013) propose the introduction of alternative species combinations to rehabilitate the land to a usable, sustainable post-mining state. Legal requirements differ across jurisdictions; in some cases, rehabilitation requires restoration to pre-disturbance land use or ecosystems (Grant et al., 2016), whereas in others different levels of biodiversity and ecosystem functioning is open to negotiation between regulatory authorities or with broader stakeholders, including local communities (Doley & Audet, 2013;Grant et al., 2016). Similar to mine closure, an integrated and iterative approach to rehabilitation is required to ensure all factors are accounted for and rehabilitation is effective and sustainable (Grant et al., 2016). According to Grant et al. (2016), rehabilitation should achieve three key objectives:
• The sustainability of land use, soil and water quality and availability.
• The partial or full repair of ecosystem functionality to reinstate biodiversity, and provision of ecosystem services for local communities.
• The minimisation of pollution of neighbouring communities and environments.

Ultimately, rehabilitation activities aim to reinstate fully functioning ecosystems and restore land productivity, although this may differ from original land-use and species composition pre-mining (Grant et al., 2016).

div.head: Mine Closure in South Africa
div.p: This research focuses on South Africa in particular, given its heavy economic reliance on the extractives industry (Crous, 2020). Additionally, South Africa possesses an extensive history of mine abandonment, and numerous mines are anticipated to cease operations in the upcoming decade (Crous, 2020), making it particularly important to understand current closure practices and identify opportunities for improvement to achieve sustainable and effective transitions post-closure.

Currently, the existing literature indicates that both regulations and disclosure norms are not posing significant challenges or inducing substantial changes in industry practices to attain successful mine closure and rehabilitation.

For many years now, mining has occupied a prominent role in South Africa's economy, and continues to do so (Utembe et al., 2015;Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016;Crous, 2020). Despite the significant contribution of mining activities to economic growth and local livelihoods, mining is associated with various negative social and ecological impacts, such as loss of vegetation, destruction of ecosystems, water contamination, abandoned mining towns, and increased social conflicts (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016;Edwards & Maritz, 2019;Mfune et al., 2020). South Africa, unfortunately, has a history of mismanaging mine closure and mitigation of the negative social, economic, and environmental consequences of mine closure by failing to implement structural economic change (Perkins et al., 2020). Consequently, South Africa can boast very few, if any, examples of successfully implemented mine closure and rehabilitation activities (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020).

Reasons for this include inadequate stakeholder engagement, concerns around residual risks and liabilities, lack of clearly defined responsibilities, the potentially high costs associated with rehabilitation, and the complexity of closure legislation and best practice guidelines (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016;Watson & Olalde, 2019). In addition, responsibilities related to mine closure and rehabilitation are commonly avoided in South Africa through a process referred to as "on-selling" (Perkins et al., 2020). Larger mining companies have traditionally sold their mining assets to smaller companies that do not have the capacity to implement effective mine closure, often resulting in mine abandonment (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020). Further, there is an apparent lack of capacity and motivation from the mining companies themselves to sustainably and successfully rehabilitate and close down mines (Watson & Olalde, 2019). Despite these impacts, it would be unfair to say that mining should come to an end, since the mining industry supplies the world with several important minerals and metals that can assist in the crucial and necessary transition to a low carbon economy (Zhou et al., 2016). Instead, the mining industry should focus on more sustainable methods of mining and sustainable closure to reduce the negative social and environmental impacts associated with the sector.

div.head: Implications of ineffective mine closure
div.p: Due to South Africa's extended reliance on mining, the evidence of ineffective mine closure is reflected in the multitude of abandoned mines present throughout the country (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Current evidence suggests that thousands of mines have been abandoned without adequate rehabilitation, with many more facing imminent closure or being sold to less well-resourced companies to close (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Edwards & Maritz, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020).

Abandoned mines are often a significant source of environmental and social problems in South Africa (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). The most common issues associated with abandoned mines include environmental stresses and pollution, public health and safety concerns, job losses, and related social-ecological impacts (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Additionally, abandoned mines attract small-scale and illegal mining activities, which results in both environmental and physical hazards to surrounding communities and ecosystems (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Considering the environmental and social repercussions resulting from inadequate closure and rehabilitation in South Africa, it becomes clear that a reevaluation and enhancement of mine closure legislation and policy implementation is necessary (Mpanza et al., 2021).

div.head: Regulatory frameworks guiding mine closure in South Africa
div.p: Historically, mining in South Africa was governed by weak regulatory systems, which placed the responsibility of mining impacts on mine owners, resulting in the thousands of abandoned mines across South Africa today (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). The regulations also permitted mining companies to abandon mines, frequently transferring the duty of mine closure and rehabilitation to governments and local communities (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016).
Additionally, mining companies also made use of unsound mining practices with little regard for the environment and often abandoned unrehabilitated mines prior to liquidation or departing the country

(Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). The Minerals Act (Act 50 of 1991) was the first step in changing the regulatory landscape for mining activities in South Africa (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). In 2002, new mining legislation, the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA), was promulgated in South Africa. This new legislation introduced stricter environmental regulations for the mining industry (Marais & de Lange, 2021). The MPRDA implemented stricter control over mining processes and the rehabilitation of mines on closure, introducing the theory of restoring the mined site to its pre-mining condition (Marais & de Lange, 2021).

Upon the conclusion of a mine's operational lifespan, South African mining companies are legally obliged to engage in closure activities as stipulated by law. These activities aim to establish postclosure land purposes that garner approval not only from the mine itself but also from neighboring communities, as well as stakeholders who experience direct or indirect impacts (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Furthermore, the activities undertaken to achieve post-closure should aim to achieve acceptable levels of environmental and social risk exposure as stipulated in the regulations (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Currently, mine closure in South Africa is regulated in terms of the National Environmental Management Act (NEMA), read together with the Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations, the Financial Provisioning Regulations in terms of NEMA and the MPRDA. The Financial Provisioning Regulations, first promulgated and operationalised in 2015, prompted mining companies to reconsider how to plan effectively for closure. As per the regulations, the responsibility for liabilities rests with the mine owner until the issuance of a closure certificate (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Further, the regulations require mine owners to make financial provisions for all environmental responsibilities related to the mine (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). The Financial Provisioning Regulations require mining companies to produce the following (Edwards & Maritz, 2019):
• A risk assessment report that evaluates the potential financial obligations linked to the postclosure management of environmental liabilities.
• An annual rehabilitation plan which reflects the activities undertaken for concurrent rehabilitation and remediation of the site.
A final rehabilitation plan that identifies and assesses post-mining land use for the mine site.

When discussing the regulatory requirements of mine closure, it is also important to mention the 2021 Draft National Mine Closure Strategy. Whilst this document is a strategy and not law, the requirements set out in the strategy may influence best practice in South Africa. Importantly, the draft strategy acknowledges that the "closure of mines typically results in often irreversible environmental degradation and economic hardship in mining-dependent community" (Draft National Mine Closure Strategy, 2021). This draft strategy indicates a positive step in adequately addressing the social and ecological challenges associated with mine closure. Although regulatory progress has been made from an environmental perspective and the regulations now hold mine owners responsible for environmental liabilities in accordance with the MPRDA and NEMA, very little consideration is given to the negative social impacts of mine closure, as well as guidance for successful social transitioning post-closure (Edwards & Maritz, 2019;Marais & de Lange, 2021).

Despite regulatory progress, certain social instruments devised by the government to support mine closure and rehabilitation are still considered inadequate (Perkins et al., 2020). While the South African regulations have considered the social consequences of mine closure, including the development of Social and Labour Plans (SLPs), some actions required by SLPs contradict social transitioning objectives governed by the regulations (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). An example of this is the necessity for mines to tackle the housing and living conditions of their employees during operational phases as outlined in their SLP, without taking into consideration the post-closure consequences this may cause (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). The provision of housing in mining communities by mining companies rarely considers the long-term consequences and social disruption that can result from downscaling of operations or mine closure (Edwards & Maritz, 2019).

Additionally, ineffective mine closure could limit households to a location that is not, and cannot, be economically viable (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Despite increased awareness of the need to promote and invest in alternative livelihoods ahead of mine closure, the guidelines governing mine-community development during mine closure has proven weak and ineffective (Perkins et al., 2020). In many cases, SLPs have become a way to draw mines into taking responsibility for municipal service delivery for surrounding communities (Perkins et al., 2020). As a result, much needed resources are diverted from the design of interventions needed to ensure long-term sustainability of surrounding communities after operational mining has come to an end (Perkins et al., 2020).

South African legislation expects that mine downscaling will reduce the negative impacts on the environment and communities, but often, the reverse is the case (Marais & de Lange, 2021). Contrary to expectations, the downsizing of mining activities has been discovered to lead to an increase in urban sprawl within South African mining towns (Marais & de Lange, 2021). This is due to several factors, including disturbances caused by boom-and-bust cycles, as well as inadequate municipal planning following the transfer of responsibilities from mines, amongst others (Marais & de Lange, 2021). Consequently, researchers and other stakeholders often advocate for early planning by governments, mining companies, and communities. This planning involves diversifying economies and identifying alternative land uses for mining towns after mining activities, aiming to mitigate the adverse effects linked to mine closure (Andrews-Speed, Ma, Shao, & Liao, 2005;World Bank, 2002).

However, if social considerations are not clearly stipulated or accounted for in the regulations, mining companies are not under any obligation to plan for diversified economies or alternative post-mining land uses (Marais & de Lange, 2021). When considering the legislation governing mine closure in South Africa, Edwards and Maritz (2019:306) note "the softer issues like rehabilitation, mine closure and community development have not received the attention they deserve". Evidence suggests that there is a need in South Africa for further guidelines to be developed and implemented to address all liabilities of mine closure, from a social transitioning perspective, as well as from an environmental resilience perspective (Edwards & Maritz, 2019).

div.head: Lack of clarity around the end goal of mine closures
div.p: Based on the available literature, South Africa is falling behind in terms of executing efficient mine closure practices and establishing comprehensive regulations for proper rehabilitation (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Uncertainty around what constitutes a "sustainable end state", as defined in the Financial Provisioning Regulations, is considered an area of regulatory uncertainty obstructing effective mine closure and rehabilitation in South Africa (Perkins et al., 2020). The requirement to mitigate the negative social impacts of mine closure outside the mine site, raises concerns about the regulations which only focuses on the environmental risk threshold of a mine site post-closure (Perkins et al., 2020). Further, consultative processes with stakeholders directly or indirectly impacted by mine closure are rarely inclusive enough to result in sustainable social-transitioning postclosure (Perkins et al., 2020). Perkins et al. (2020) argue that surrounding communities are excluded from engagements on mine closure and rehabilitation planning, regardless of whether it addresses support for post-closure livelihood development or not (Perkins et al., 2020). These factors limit South Africa's ability to achieve successful mine closure and post-closure rehabilitation of impacted communities and ecosystems.

As an increasing number of large-scale mines reach operational end of life, mine closure becomes a shared concern globally (Crous, 2020). What is clear is that mine closure is not an isolated event, it poses a challenge for governments, companies, and mine-affected communities alike (Crous, 2020).

Concerningly for South Africa, imperatives for decarbonisation, in line with the country's commitments under the Paris Agreement, are increasing pressure to reduce the country's dependence on coal-generated power (Perkins et al., 2020). As a result, mine closure in coal-producing areas becomes inevitable (Perkins et al., 2020). The closure of coal-producing mines will result in largescale job losses within the mines and the coal-fired power stations they serve, as well as amongst the range of businesses that provide goods and services to coal mines (Perkins et al., 2020).

Consequently, mine closure will impact heavily on surrounding communities, causing an increase in household vulnerability and food insecurity (Perkins et al., 2020). These impacts also increase surrounding communities' vulnerability to external shocks such as those caused by a changing climate. As such, ensuring transformative and sustainable mine closure and rehabilitation is crucial for building social and ecological resilience to climate change impacts beyond the life of mine.

div.head: Climate change and the mining sector
div.p: Pearce et al. (2011) argue that climate change is a critical environmental threat and business risk within the mining sector. When considering the latest future scenarios of climate change for example, it is evident that many areas across South Africa will be exposed to increasing occurrences of climate change impacts, such as increasing temperatures and flash flooding (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021).
This, in turn, will have an impact on the operational processes of mines scattered across South Africa.

Moreover, and central to this research, climate change impacts will affect the adaptive capacity of the environment and communities surrounding the mine, reducing social and ecological resilience, and exacerbating existing social vulnerabilities, particularly after mine closure. As such, successful mine closure planning requires strong climate change adaptation plans to prepare for future climate change risks and to strengthen social and ecological resilience post-closure. The degree to which the mining sector can mitigate its own harmful impact, whilst simultaneously adapting to climate change impacts, will influence the long-term success of the mine, and impact the economic prosperity of host communities post-closure (Pearce et al., 2011). Further, Pearce et al. (2011) highlight several important findings within the mining sector: a) currently, limited adaptation planning is being adopted for projected climate change impacts, and b) extensive vulnerabilities exist post-closure. These findings highlight the necessary gap for my intended research.

div.head: Extended influence of mines
div.p: Due to South Africa's historical reliance on the mining sector, mining towns and communities are common occurrences across South Africa (Marais et al., 2020). In South Africa, mining communities are home to 5.4 million people and are predominantly located in coal, gold, platinum, and diamond mining areas (Cole & Broadhurst, 2020). This is an indication of the extensive influence that a mine has on surrounding communities, as well as the magnitude of impact when the mine vacates an area.

Managing the entire life cycle of a mine is a complex and major concern for mining companies (Marais et al., 2020). Consequently, successful mine closure and rehabilitation remain problematic in South Africa, despite legislation that should ensure success (Perkins et al., 2020). Systemic challenges, including a disconnect between policy and legislation and the way in which this is implemented, threaten the successful implementation of mine closure, rehabilitation, and the identification of viable land uses necessary for the development of alternative livelihoods (Perkins et al., 2020). Even in cases where mine closure is achieved, employees and host communities are often stranded without alternative forms of employment or income generation post-closure (Perkins et al., 2020). Hence, collaboration with impacted stakeholder groups is important to achieve sustainable social-transitions post-closure.

div.head: The Impact of Mine Closure on Communities and Ecosystems
Transitioning to suitable land uses
div.p: Operational mining is acknowledged as a temporary land use (Manero et al., 2020). As such, the closure of a mine is inevitable. As a result, planning for closure and rehabilitation should encompass the transition towards appropriate post-mining land uses, as this is essential for restoring ecosystems, preserving biodiversity, and supporting local livelihoods (Simoni & Leite, 2019;Manero et al., 2020).

As discussed above, rehabilitation typically aims to restore the mining land to its historical ecosystem, or an agreed upon alternative land-use (Manero et al., 2020). As per Brent and Fourie (2008), mine closure presents two main challenges: environmental rehabilitation and the dependence of local communities on ongoing mining operations. Failing to rehabilitate properly during or after closure can result in environmental degradation that infringes upon the rights of ecosystems and the neighboring communities (Mpanza et al., 2021). Environmental rights include the provision of ecosystem services such as food, water, health, and usable land (Mpanza et al., 2021). Within the mining landscape, the environment and community are inextricably interlinked, in other words one cannot function optimally without the other. To mitigate social and ecological challenges, it is important for mine closure and rehabilitation to be considered a long-term, integrated planning process intended to minimise enduring environmental and social effects, rather than being viewed solely as a procedure at the end of a project's life (Mpanza et al., 2021).

div.head: The negative impacts of mining
div.p: There is sufficient evidence to suggest that mining has transformed several economies across the world (Worlanyo & Jiangfeng, 2021). However, mining has also negatively impacted on the environment, affecting the resilience of ecosystems and, ultimately, surrounding communities (Simoni & Leite, 2019;Worlanyo & Jiangfeng, 2021). Negative environmental impacts of mining activities, which can also pose challenges to surrounding communities, include loss of vegetation, loss of biodiversity and ecosystem degradation, irreparable destruction of water sources, land-use changes, and food insecurity, amongst others (Worlanyo & Jiangfeng, 2021). As a result, unless properly planned for and implemented, mine closure, or mine abandonment, can result in significant environmental, social, and economic consequences (Mudder & Harvey, 1999;Swart, 2003;Limpitlaw, 2004;Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Major factors that contribute to social and ecological challenges caused by mining activities include the type of commodity mined, the mining method used, and the location of the mine (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016; Watson & Olalde, 2019). This discrepancy arises because the land disturbances resulting from surface mining differ significantly from those caused by underground mining operations. However, in both cases, there is often a substantial impact beyond the mining rights area, characterized by pollution and the accumulation of waste materials from the mine (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016).

Although the mining sector has made significant strides to minimise the environmental impacts caused by mining activities and planning for efficient rehabilitation, many abandoned mines still exist, which remain a major environmental challenge (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016).

Common physical and environmental impacts caused by ineffective mine closure and abandoned mines include altered landscapes, degraded ecosystem and biodiversity functioning, land no longer viable because of a loss or contamination of soil, abandoned waste disposal facilities, changes in ground and surface water quality, and changes in vegetation cover (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Water resources are often the most frequently polluted through ineffective mine closure activities or by abandoned mines, which in turn has consequential impacts for surrounding communities (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016), again highlighting the interlinked relationship between the environment and communities.

div.head: Social challenges associated with mine closure
div.p: Often overlooked are the social challenges associated with mine closure. According to Bainton and Holcombe (2018), there is more information available on the environmental and physical aspects of mine closure compared to the social aspects. Furthermore, as highlighted in Crous's (2020) examination of four major mining companies, there is a significant scarcity of information pertaining to the social facets of mine closure within publicly available reporting documents. However, for mine closure planning is crucial in accounting for the full range of social, environmental, and economic costs and risks associated with mining activities and, ultimately, closure and rehabilitation due to the interdependent relationship found between the environment and communities (Bainton & Holcombe, 2018).

According to Worlanyo and Jiangfeng (2021:12), "mining contributes substantial adverse effects to society vis-a-vis its positive impacts". In other words, mining results in more negative social consequences than positive impacts. Negative social impacts on mining communities include high crime rates and conflict, displacement of families and farmlands, increased migration to mining communities leading to higher prices of goods and services, and the destruction of ecosystems which limits the provision of ecosystem services to communities (Worlanyo & Jiangfeng, 2021). In some instances, a whole community can be displaced by mining activities due to a loss of farmlands, contaminated water, fire outbreaks or high toxicity of the environment due to mining waste or pollution incidents (Worlanyo & Jiangfeng, 2021). Mining operations are intricately linked to surrounding communities and ecosystems (ICMM, 2022). Nevertheless, the social dimensions of mining have always posed a challenge to the mining and extractives industry (Bainton & Holcolmbe, 2018).

Social challenges and impacts become particularly critical towards the end of a mine's operational life, when several challenges align at once (Bainton & Holcolmbe, 2018). Challenges that emerge toward the end of life include financial constraints, unfinished socio-economic development, and increased challenges associated with legacy issuesfoot_1 (Bainton & Holcolmbe, 2018). Consequently, mine closure can have significant adverse impacts on local communities, contributing further to poverty and impoverishment, loss of key services and employment, and large scale out-migration (Bainton & Holcolmbe, 2018;Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Inadequately planned for and poorly managed mine closure, or mine abandonment, can exacerbate these impacts and cause long-term adverse consequences for surrounding communities (Bainton & Holcolmbe, 2018). Further, as has been established by this literature review, social vulnerabilities, such as those caused by ineffective mine closure or abandonment, make communities more vulnerable to climate change impacts. When a mine is closed, the surrounding communities often experience distress and frustration (Mpanza et al., 2021). Distress caused by mine closure is due to job loss, safety issues, ill health, and the contamination of surrounding environments, compromising the availability of ecosystem services (Mpanza et al., 2021).

div.head: Socio-economic benefits of mining
div.p: Due to the profitable nature of mining, operational activities bring substantial investments to surrounding communities, thereby contributing significantly to the socio-economic development of host communities (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Socio-economic benefits of mining include new job opportunities, infrastructure development, and supply of basic needs such as running water, electricity, building of schools and health care facilities (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Often a mine is the primary provider of income, employment, and service delivery within surrounding communities, leading to increased social pressure in the lead up to mine closure (Limpitlaw, 2004). Additionally, the socio-economic benefits associated with mining activities result in an influx of people and the rapid expansion of new communities around mine sites (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). Consequently, communities within the vicinity of operational mines continue to be a concern during and post-closure because they become dependent on the economic opportunities created by the mine (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). As such, abandoned mines are often found amongst densely populated communities, increasing the community's vulnerability to external shocks, such as those caused by climate change (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016).

div.head: The consequences of failed mine closure
div.p: Ineffective mine closure or abandonment can significantly impact the quality of life and livelihood of people remaining after closure (Limpitlaw, 2004;Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). This impact is significantly worse in developing countries where local governments often lack the capacity or ability to provide alternative economic opportunities or assume the responsibility of services such as local emergency, education, or health services (Limpitlaw, 2004;Edwards & Maritz, 2019). This situation arises either due to the prior provision of services by the mining company or as a consequence of diminished government revenues (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Interestingly, in certain instances, mining companies assume the role of the local municipality by providing surrounding communities with basic services, such as water and refuge collection (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). The mining company believes it is providing socio-economic benefits for local communities. However, the issue arises post-closure when the local municipality is once again responsible for service delivery but lacks the capacity, leaving the community exposed and vulnerable to external shocks (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Additionally, external shocks are often exacerbated by existing vulnerabilities within communities, such as a high prevalence of informal settlements, a high HIV/AIDs rate, as well as chronic and acute malnutrition (Mhlango & Amponsah-Dacosta, 2016). These vulnerabilities make local communities more susceptible to the negative impacts of climate change.

div.head: The importance of community engagement
div.p: It is evident that significant strides need to be taken to integrate social challenges into mine closure planning and rehabilitation, thereby guaranteeing the continued prosperity of sustainable communities long after the mine ceases operations (Stevens, 2021). This is particularly relevant, given that the people who live in the vicinity of the mine are expected to experience the most pronounced effects due to the social, economic, and environmental shifts brought about by the closure (Stevens, 2021). To ensure productive and safe post-mining land use and thriving communities, local governments and mining companies should ensure that community members, both from a local and regional level, are actively and equally involved in closure discussions, from initial planning to postclosure monitoring (Stevens, 2021). Community involvement in mine closure and rehabilitation planning is also crucial for the development and implementation of climate change adaptation responses post-closure (Rankoana, 2020). Community-based adaptation enables individuals to prepare for and handle the effects of climate change by emphasizing processes guided by community perspectives, needs, knowledge, and capabilities (Midgley et al., 2012). Rankoana (2020) asserts that, integrating community-based adaptation into climate change policies and strategies could assist in developing a better understanding of climate change, its impacts, and local responses that could be used for adaptation. This could assist communities in the mine's vicinity to better prepare for, and respond to, climate change impacts (Rankoana, 2020).

Another approach for effective post-closure transitioning involves enhancing the resilience of the surrounding communities in preparation for closure (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Resilience can help mining-affected communities adapt and respond to changes or stress brought about by mine closure (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). Moreover, building resilience helps communities in better managing external stresses and disturbances such as climate change impacts (Edwards & Maritz, 2019).

Considering climate change impacts in the design and planning of settlements, both urban and rural, is crucial for resilience building and enhancing social well-being (Langsdorf et al., 2022). Hence, it could be beneficial to include climate change adaptation in mine closure planning and rehabilitation to build social and ecological resilience amongst mine-impacted communities and environments. The mining industry holds significant potential to support and accelerate community development by acting as a catalyst for social and economic change (ICMM, 2022). Nonetheless, for development to be inclusive and sustainable all stakeholders, from government to industry, need to collaborate to encourage diversification of the economy beyond mining, and to improve communities' resilience to external shocks (ICMM, 2022).

With increasing impacts of climate change already evident in South Africa, it becomes important to prepare for future impacts, specifically within vulnerable social and ecological systems, such as those often found surrounding operational mines in South Africa. Climate change impacts could be substantially worse for surrounding communities and the environment by the time the operational life of a mine comes to an end, underscoring the importance for mining companies to consider climate change adaptation options during mine closure planning and rehabilitation.

div.head: Social-Ecological Systems
div.p: Given that I recognise the impact of closure on both social and ecological systems, I explore the concept of social-ecological systems (SES) by emphasizing the interconnected nature and need to address closure holistically. The concept of SES recognizes that social and ecological elements interact, and places an emphasis on the "human-in-nature" viewpoint (Daron et al., 2015;Petrosillo et al., 2015). In other words, SESs are not simply understood to be social plus ecological systems, but rather intimately interlinked systems that are characterised by clear connections and feedbacks across both social and ecological components (Folke et al., 2010;Biggs, Schlüter, and Schoon 2015 in Biggs et al., 2022). There are several guiding principles that underpin the concept of SES thinking (Preiser et al., 2018), most importantly, social, and ecological systems support, connect and interact with each other in a myriad of ways that are vital for social and ecological resilience.

While the study of SESs focuses on acknowledging and comprehending the connection between human beings and the environment, ecosystem services constitute a significant subset of these interactions (Biggs et al., 2022). Ecosystem services refer to benefits that are derived from nature for the benefit of human life and livelihoods (Mengist, Soromessa & Feyisa, 2020). Mine communities in rural areas in South Africa still rely heavily on ecosystem-services. Examples of ecosystem services include mangroves, fields, forests, rivers, and oceans that provide food, fuel, and water. On the one hand, society depends on the environment for life-sustaining benefits; on the other hand, it is society's practices that are changing ecosystems in profound and uncertain ways on a global scale (Fischer et al., 2015). This is a clear example of the complex and interacting nature of SESs. Human interference, although well-intended, can have negative consequences for natural ecosystems, and this is because SESs are complex systems. Simply, change affecting society will have a corresponding effect on the environment and vice versa. Fischer et al. (2015) argue that the concept of SESs has facilitated increased recognition of the human dependence on the environment, as well as the development of policy frameworks that consider social-ecological interactions. However, meeting social needs whilst simultaneously protecting ecosystems and the benefits they offer, is still considered a global challenge (Leslie et al., 2015).

Furthermore, environmental challenges, such as climate change impacts, are testing the capabilities of current social-ecological management practices (Virapongse et al., 2016). These challenges are pushing the demand for innovative approaches to SESs management. Further, there is an increased call for the integration of natural and social systems when developing approaches for addressing a range of ecological and societal impacts, including climate change impacts (Virapongse et al., 2016).

Closely linked to the concept of SESs and the theory of ecosystem services is nature-based solutions and, more importantly for this research study, ecosystem-based adaptation. Nature-based solutions encompass strategies aimed at safeguarding, responsibly overseeing, and revitalising both unaltered and altered ecosystems. These approaches adeptly and flexibly tackle societal dilemmas while concurrently promoting mutual advantages for both human communities and the environment (Potschin et al., 2016). Similarly, ecosystem-based adaptation revolves around harnessing biodiversity and ecosystem services to support communities in adjusting to the uncertainties brought about by a changing climate system (Seddon et al., 2020). Nature-based solutions have gained increasing attention over the past several years as an effective adaptation response to climate change impacts. According to the World Resources Institute (WRI), nature-based solutions can play an important role in managing climate change impacts, whilst generating environmental, economic, and social benefits (Tye et al., 2022). From the perspective of SESs theory, the link between the health of ecosystems and human resilience is evident. However, what is also evident is that when ecosystems are degraded, vital ecosystem services provided by nature become limited, amplifying societies' vulnerability to climate change impacts (Tye et al., 2022). It has been suggested that nature-based solutions can increase societies' resilience to climate change impacts by building adaptive capacity to hazards such as flooding, drought, and water scarcity, as well as protecting and sustaining livelihoods and well-being (Tye et al., 2022). The following section unpacks this theory in detail.

div.head: The Need for Climate Change Adaptation in South Africa
div.p: Providing an overview of climate change impacts is important to this study as it highlight the risks associated to a specific region. These risks should guide mining companies in developing closure and rehabilitation strategies, as these impacts continue to affect social-ecological systems long after a mine has been decommissioned. However, it is important to note that this research is not about unpacking these impacts in depth, given their extensive coverage in climate change literature. This review highlights the need for climate action across multiple sectors, including the mining industry, particularly post-closure.

The impacts of climate change are increasingly being felt around the world (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021). Changing rainfall and temperature patterns, among other changes, are affecting both ecosystems and human societies in diverse ways (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021). Climate change has societal impacts such as flash flooding, increased frequency of droughts and heat waves, while ecosystem impacts experience effects like habitat and coral reef loss, among other impacts. According to the World Economic Forum's (WEF) Global Risks Report (2022), amongst the highest likelihood risks of the next ten years are climate action failure, extreme weather, and biodiversity loss (WEF, 2022). As a result, climate change adaptation is becoming increasingly important on both a global and local scale (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021). Climate change impacts disproportionately affect developing countries (van der Bank & Karsten, 2020). This is because developing countries do not possess the means to cope with the climatic hazards associated with climate change, often due to existing social and economic challenges (van der Bank & Karsten, 2020). According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) latest climate report, between 1.5°C and 2°C global warming will result in severe consequences for food production, economic growth, inequality and poverty, biodiversity, and human morbidity and mobility in Africa in particular (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021). It is contended that the magnitude of exposure and vulnerability to climate change impacts in Africa is due to a multi-dimensional interplay between social, political, and environmental factors (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021).

Further, African citizens are disproportionately employed by climate-exposed sectors, such as agriculture, mining and rainfed cropland, exacerbating the continent's vulnerability to climate change impacts. Some of the more concerning social risks the continent faces include water stress, a decline in food security and a loss in agricultural productivity (Rankoana, 2020). On the other hand, the continent also faces environmental risks such as habitat destruction, ecosystem degradation, and declining wildlife populations, amongst others (Rankoana, 2020). For these reasons, it is important for developing countries to keep climate change adaptation at the forefront of sustainable development strategies (van der Bank & Karsten, 2020).
South Africa's economy, for example, is highly reliant on both mining and agriculture, thereby increasing the country's exposure to climate change impacts (Rankoana, 2020). For this reason, South

Africa is appropriate for unpacking the impacts of climate change on mining communities due to the economy's substantial reliance on the mining sector and the prevalence of vulnerable communities across the country. Ziervogel et al. (2014) contend that climate change is a key concern for South Africa. Some of the most noticeable impacts of climate change in South Africa to date is the increased frequency of extreme weather events, such as droughts, wildfires, and flash flooding (Chersich & Wright, 2019). Additionally, increasing temperatures have a marked effect on occupational settings in South Africa, particularly in the mining and agricultural sectors (Chersich & Wright, 2019).

Coupled with this, the impacts of increasing temperatures, including mortality, disproportionately affect people living in informal settlements across South Africa due to the prevalence of corrugated iron constructed housing. South Africa's water resources, food security, health, infrastructure, as well as social-ecological systems are all significantly threatened by these projected climate change impacts (Ziervogel et al., 2014;Chersich & Wright, 2019). Hence the need for an increased focus on climate change adaptation in South Africa, particularly amongst vulnerable communities and ecosystems such as those surrounding operational mines.

As mentioned in the previous section, social-ecological systems are an important component of this study, as climate change, ecosystem degradation and environmental changes are underpinned by a multifaceted and interrelating system of social changes, which in turn are influenced by the environment and environmental disruptions (Biggs et al., 2022). Importantly, the sustenance of human societies hinges on the living elements present in natural systems (Pecl et al., 2017). Climatedriven changes to ecosystems and natural environments affect human populations both directly, such as through the emergence of diseases and shifts in food supply, as well as indirectly, such as through ecosystem degradation (Pecl et al., 2017). The following section unpacks the concept of nature-based solutions as an adaptation response to projected climate change impacts.

div.head: Nature-based Solutions
div.p: One method of reducing the impact of climatic shocks is through climate change adaptation (Fankhauser, 2017). Adaptation solutions need to be considered to avoid catastrophic social, economic, and environmental impacts of climate change, such as flash flooding, drought, fires, and other extreme weather events (Langsdorf et al., 2022). Simply put, climate change adaptation occurs when reducing vulnerability or enhancing resilience to projected climate change impacts (Fankhauser, 2017). It is about helping people, economies and ecosystems thrive in the face of increasing temperatures. According to Moser and Ekstrom (2010:22026), "adaptation involves changes in social-ecological systems in response to actual and expected impacts of climate change in the context of interacting non-climatic changes". In other words, climate change adaptation requires certain changes in social-ecological systems to reduce the systems' exposure to projected impacts.

div.head: Exploring adaptation responses
div.p: Adaptation responses can take a variety of shapes and forms, depending on the context of a community, country, or region (Owen, 2020). Furthermore, present adaptation strategies rely on the various and interconnecting manners in which society comprehends, encounters, and reacts to climate change (Owen, 2020). Although adaptation responses have progressed over the past two decades, there remains several challenges in both implementing and measuring effective adaptation (Owen, 2020). Engle (2011) suggests that the disagreement over the practice of adaptation is primarily driven by the difficulty in defining the fundamental goals of adaptation. Owen (2020) highlights three defining objectives of adaptation: (1) increasing adaptive capacity in order to respond effectively to climatic shocks; (2) increasing resilience or the ability of a social-ecological system to functioning effectively after experiencing a climatic shock; and lastly (3) reducing vulnerability or harm when confronted with an external shock. Smit and Wandel (2006) explain that the three objectives of adaptation are often interconnected. However, with countless definitions describing these objectives, they can become over simplified when applied without context (Smit & Wandel, 2006). In summary, the literature emphasizes the intricacies of defining adaptation, delineating its objectives, and illustrating successful advancement toward achieving those objectives.

div.head: Defining climate change adaptation
div.p: As such, climate change adaptation is a multi-faceted challenge, which requires adequate knowledge, planning, coordination, and foresight (Fankhauser, 2017). According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP, 2019) and the UNFCCC (2021), adaptation not only requires a response to current climate impacts but also needs to assist society to prepare for future impacts.

Further, adaptation must address uncertainty (UNEP, 2019). A myriad of uncertainties exists when considering climate change adaptation options, including scientific uncertainty about projected changes and impacts, technical uncertainty about the effectiveness of implemented solutions, socioeconomic uncertainty about the impact on livelihoods and social functioning, political uncertainty about policy and institutional changes, and, lastly, financial uncertainty about funding adaptation (Pelling, 2011;UNEP, 2019). Importantly, Fankhauser (2017) highlights that climate change adaptation is a long-term, iterative process. In other words, adaptation responses need to have a longterm horizon, coupled with the need to be constantly evolving to ensure improvements and provision of adequate adaptive capacity to projected and actual impacts.

div.head: Adaptation solutions employing nature
div.p: There is a growing awareness that climate change adaptation solutions can be found in nature, which has given rise to the theory of nature-based solutions (NbS) (UNEP, 2019). NbS were a key topic during COP26 in November 2021, and it became apparent during the conference that climate change impacts cannot be tackled without nature (Tye et al., 2022). NbS is key to responding to climate change in a way that addresses the complexities of SESs, unlike more traditional climate adaptation solutions. It has been established that society's vulnerability to climate change impacts is intimately connected to our dependency on ecosystem services, or the inability of ecosystems to provide crucial services due to climatic and non-climatic degradation (Doswald & Osti, 2011;Kabisch et al., 2016).

Consequently, more recent adaption responses have been focused on a decision between measures that stabilise or enhance ecosystem services ("green" infrastructure) and those that mimic or supplement these functions with engineered approaches ("grey" infrastructure) (Doswald & Osti, 2011;Kabisch et al., 2016).

Emerging evidence suggests that NbS can provide low-cost alternatives to climate change impacts and, in some contexts, offer key advantages over engineered approaches (Seddon et al., 2020). There is a growing consensus amongst experts to implement a combined approach to adaptation by making use of both green and grey infrastructure to adapt to climate change impacts (Seddon et al., 2020).

As such, NbS offer an appropriate strategy, alongside other options, to aid adaptation to climate change impacts, as well as assist in slowing global warming, supporting biodiversity, and securing the provision of ecosystem services (Seddon et al., 2020). Although climate change adaptation reduces social risk and vulnerability to climate change impacts, it fails to prioritise both nature and people. Recognising that social and ecological systems are intertwined and deeply dependent on one another, NbS can contribute to the sustainable management or restoration of natural ecosystems, effectively addressing societal challenges such as climate change, human health, food and water
