This approach simultaneously offers benefits for both human well-being and biodiversity (World Bank Group, 2022). As such, NbS can prove to be important in the context of mine closure and rehabilitation, as mining impacts both social and ecological systems simultaneously.

NbS are adaptation responses that aim to reduce or reverse ecosystem degradation and tackle societal challenges, whilst simultaneously supporting and enriching both social and ecological systems by promoting sustainable development (Tye et al., 2022;Seddon et al., 2020). Evidence suggests that NbS can protect both social and ecological systems from climate change impacts, including from short-term and longer-term threats such as flooding and desertification respectively (Tye et al., 2022).

NbS harness the natural environment to ensure delivery of ecosystem services, along with a range of associated benefits that aid to address social, economic, and environmental challenges (Sarabi et al., 2019). An example of a NbS for climate change adaptation is the expansion of urban forests and green spaces in cities to curb rising temperatures and heat waves (Tye et al., 2022). Initially, the concept of NbS was focused on enhancing social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts, however the broader potential of NbS to address a wide range of socioeconomic challenges, as well as environmental challenges, has been increasingly recognised (Sarabi et al., 2019). As an illustration, farmers in Kenya who embraced conservation agriculture practices -such as minimizing soil disturbance and employing crop rotation for soil health -experienced improved land and labor productivity, along with substantial cost reductions (Wekesa et al., 2018).

div.head: Adaptation responses anchored in nature
div.p: NbS encompass a broad spectrum of adaptive measures, spanning from safeguarding and overseeing ecosystems to integrating "green" infrastructure within urban regions and employing ecosystembased principles in agricultural systems (Seddon et al., 2020). The concept of NbS is based on the idea that healthy, well-functioning ecosystems can support the provision of a diverse range of services that support societal well-being, from controlling floods to providing clear air and clean water (Seddon et al., 2020). According to Seddon et al. (2020), NbS differ in three important ways from traditional climate change adaptation responses, which can influence the breadth of benefits provided to people and ecosystems:
• NbS encompass a broad range of interventions from protection or restoration of natural ecosystems to developing hybrid 'grey-green' approaches such as city parks or green roofs.
In other words, NbS are not limited to one form of intervention. NbS can incorporate a broad range of interventions, from both a social and ecological perspective, to adapt to climate change impacts.

• NbS exhibit diversity in their support for biodiversity, which affects their resilience and ability to adapt to shocks and hazards. NbS that center on safeguarding and restoring ecosystems can play a pivotal role in ensuring climate change mitigation and adaptation services.
Additionally, they offer cultural ecosystem services, such as fostering a connection with nature and enhancing well-being

• NbS vary in how they are designed and implemented on a localised level. In other words, NbS are a collaborative, community-based climate change adaptation strategy that takes into consideration the social, economic, environmental, and cultural intricacies of local communities.

div.head: The benefits of nature-based adaptation responses
div.p: Evidently, NbS aim to address broader societal goals that support human wellbeing, such as poverty alleviation and socioeconomic development, especially within more vulnerable sectors of society (Seddon et al., 2020). As such, NbS differ from traditional conservation and climate adaptation approaches that aim to address one aspect of either a social or ecological system (Seddon et al., 2020).

However, Sarabi et al. (2019) argue that for NbS to be resilient they must be implemented in a manner that maintains and supports both society and biodiversity. When implemented effectively, NbS offer a range of co-benefits, including boosting the resilience of social-ecological systems by strengthening their ability to adapt to various shocks, such as flooding, heatwaves, coastal erosion, and more (Sarabi et al., 2019).

NbS can provide a range of benefits to society and nature simultaneously (Tye et al., 2022). Benefits of NbS include sequestering and storing carbon, assisting society to adapt to the impacts of climate change, enhancing societal health and wellbeing, providing a source of income, and protecting the environment and boosting biodiversity (Tye et al., 2022). NbS can also offer adaptation benefits (Nelson, 2011). The advantages of collaborating with ecosystems for adaptation purposes include shielding communities from or diminishing their vulnerability to climate change impacts, ensuring the consistent provision of essential ecosystem services that society relies upon, preserving existing livelihoods and income sources even in the face of climate impacts, and establishing new avenues for livelihoods to replace those endangered by climatic shocks (Nelson, 2011).

Moreover, an analysis conducted by Sarabi et al. (2019) identified the far-reaching socio-economic benefits of NbS. Evidence suggested that NbS have the potential to bring different stakeholders together to initiate social interventions for the benefit of society and the environment (Sarabi et al., 2019). Interestingly, NbS have demonstrated a growing efficacy in fostering ecosystem stewardship and cultivating a sense of belonging within affected communities, including those vulnerable populations and low-income groups that are often underrepresented (Sarabi et al., 2019). Due to these benefits, NbS form a crucial role in integrated sustainable development strategies (Seddon et al., 2020).

div.head: Challenges associated with nature-based adaptation responses
div.p: However, NbS are not without their challenges (Langsdorf et al., 2022). Inadequately implemented NbS can result in negative social, ecological, and biophysical impacts (Seddon et al., 2020). Negative side-effects of poorly implemented NbS include land grabs, human rights abuses, biodiversity loss, and water shortages (Seddon et al., 2020). Other challenges associated with NbS include difficulties in measuring effectiveness, reliability, and determining the cost-effectiveness of NbS (Seddon et al., 2020). In some cases, the benefits of NbS outweigh the cost of implementation and management, and growing evidence suggests that NbS can be more cost-effective than engineered "grey" infrastructure alternatives (Seddon et al., 2020;Tye et al., 2022). However, evidence is not well-established enough yet to determine in which contexts this is the case (Tye et al., 2022). Additionally, NbS are put under pressure with increasing climatic changes, this means we cannot solve all problems with just NbS, we must also reduce our emissions and mitigate greenhouse gas emissions. On a localised scale, NbS is beneficial, but it is not the global solution to climate change impacts (Langsdorf et al., 2022).

As the world grapples with the impacts of climate change, an opportunity exists to scale NbS initiatives as an alternative and beneficial adaptation pathway (Tye et al., 2022). Vulnerable and under-represented populations in particular stand to benefit from increased implementation of NbS (Tye et al., 2022;Sarabi et al., 2019). Evidence suggests that NbS can effectively reduce climate risks for women, the elderly, people living in poverty, people living with disabilities, and communities that depend directly on natural resources or are physically exposed to climate change impacts (Tye et al., 2022). Mining communities in South Africa are often characterised by poverty, inequality and people that rely directly on natural resources for the provision of ecosystem services (Cole and Broadhurst, 2021) thus making NbS an appropriate option for climate change adaptation strategies during mine closure.

div.head: Ecosystem-based Adaptation
div.p: Ecosystem-based adaptation, as a type of NbS, has recently gained significant importance and popularity in the context of climate change impacts (Ojea, 2015;Reid et al., 2019;UNEP, 2019).

There is increasing agreement that ecosystem degradation and the destruction of the natural environment is limiting our capacity to adapt to climate change on a global scale (Seddon et al., 2020). As such, it has been argued that ecosystem-based adaptation responses should be harnessed as a priority in the fight against climate change impacts (Seddon et al., 2020;Reid et al., 2019). This stems from the fact that ecosystem-based adaptation holds the potential to enhance adaptive capacity and social-ecological resilience to the effects of climate change in both developed and developing nations (Seddon et al., 2020). According to Reid et al. (2019), evidence suggests that ecosystembased adaptation can provide important, long-term, and far-reaching benefits in relation to climate change adaptation, the environment, and society, making it a popular alternative in adapting to climate change. Ecosystem-based adaptation approaches are distinctive from other natural resource and biodiversity management approaches as it focuses specifically on adaptation needs and benefits, and places both in the context of a broader adaptation strategy (Reid et al., 2019).

Ecosystem-based Adaptation (hereafter referred to as EbA) is a climate change adaptation strategy that harnesses nature-based solutions and ecosystem services to build resilience to climate change impacts (Langsdorf et al., 2022). EbA utilises the capacity of well-functioning biodiversity systems and ecosystem services to increase the resilience and reduce the vulnerability of both society and the environment to climate change impacts (Langsdorf et al., 2022). In other words, EbA is a natural form of climate change adaptation that enhances the existing power of the natural environment and ecosystem services to help social-ecological systems adapt to the adverse impacts of climate change.

EbA not only protects vulnerable communities from extreme weather events brought on by climate change, but also provides a variety of ecological benefits that are vital for social well-being, such as clean water and food (UNEP, 2019). It has already been established that society depends directly on ecosystems and the services they provide for their well-being (Seddon et al., 2020). As such, healthy ecosystems can play a crucial role in helping society adapt to climate change impacts, including buffering humans from direct climatic shocks (for example, flash flooding), providing vital services during changing climatic conditions, and supporting livelihoods (Seddon et al., 2020). Though primarily considered as an adaptation approach to climate change impacts, EbA can also assist in climate change mitigation by reducing carbon emissions that came about because of habitat loss and ecosystem degradation (Ojea, 2015). However, positive impacts associated with EbA depend on the effective design and implementation of adaptation interventions (Langsdorf et al., 2022). Langsdorf et al. (2022) argue that effectively designed and implemented EbA can reduce climate change risks to society and the environment, as well as maintain the provision of ecosystem services.

Effectively designed EbA interventions can help manage long-term social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts (Reid et al., 2019). An effective EbA design depends on a comprehensive understanding of the dependencies and multi-pathway links present within SESs, as well as the interactions between climatic and non-climatic ecosystem degradation (Reid et al., 2019). When designing EbA interventions, it is also important to establish how the ecosystem can support the identified adaptation objective (Reid et al., 2019). While effectively implemented EbA can reduce the impacts of climate change, at the same time, the biggest threat to EbA is climate change, with the effectiveness of EbA declining with every temperature increase (Langsdorf et al., 2022). The interconnected nature of rising temperatures and the declining effectiveness of EbA is, in my opinion, a clear example of the complexity of social-ecological systems. Ideally, implemented EbA measures should in themselves be able to withstand changing climatic conditions over the long term (Reid et al., 2019).

Evidence suggests that optimally functioning ecosystems alone cannot guarantee social-ecological resilience, as such, EbA measures need to be implemented as part of a broader adaptation strategy (Seddon et al., 2020). In each scenario, EbA interventions should be evaluated as one option amongst both engineered and hybrid approaches for climate change adaptation (Seddon et al., 2020). Further, the evaluation of each scenario should also consider the social and institutional measures relevant to the context (Seddon et al., 2020). Lastly, the costs and benefits of adaptation responses should be assessed, and benefits and trade-offs compared over space and time to select feasible options, as well as ensure equity amongst involved stakeholders (UNEP, 2019). To enhance social-ecological resilience and the ability to adapt to climate change impacts, particularly in low-income countries reliant on ecosystems and natural resources for their livelihoods, it is vital to employ participatory and community-led approaches when implementing ecosystem-based adaptation responses (Seddon et al., 2020).

Further, Seddon et al. (2020) argues that EbA can, in some cases, be more cost-effective than traditional adaptation approaches. In addition, EbA is a good option when tackling adaptation and mitigation simultaneously (Seddon et al., 2020). According to Reid et al. (2019), EbA can provide a broad range of benefits in addition to climate change adaptation, including carbon storage, pollination services and livelihood diversification. However, to reap the full potential of EbA, implementation should be a participatory process that involves close partnership and collaboration with local organisations, places an emphasis on local knowledge, and takes necessary action to manage differential benefits and trade-offs (Reid et al., 2019). Unpacking several examples of EbA helps to highlight the broader benefits associated with this method of adaptation:

div.head: Forests
div.p: The restoration and improved management of existing forests, as well as planting trees on degraded or agricultural land, provides great potential for carbon sinks (Seddon et al., 2020). In addition to the climate change mitigation potential of expanding forests, the protection and restoration of these ecosystems are also beneficial for adapting to climate change impacts (Seddon et al., 2020).

div.head: Peatlands
div.p: Peatlands are highly efficient carbon sinks (Seddon et al., 2020). Peatlands can sink carbon in perpetuity, making their protection crucial for climate change mitigation purposes (Leifeld & Menichetti, 2018). Interestingly for this research, peatlands are common ecosystems that get degraded by mining activities and mine drainage (Leifeld & Menichetti, 2018). Consequently, restoring degraded peatlands can turn these ecosystems back into carbon sinks, providing a highly cost-effective climate change mitigation strategy (Leifeld & Menichetti, 2018).

div.head: Agriculture
div.p: Responsible management of agriculture can provide soil and aboveground carbon sinks (Seddon et al., 2020). Agroforestry refers to the integration of trees into farmland and enhances the carbon sink rate of croplands or pastures, simultaneously boosting biodiversity, supporting livelihoods, and reducing soil degradation (Seddon et al., 2020). Other forms of nature-based agricultural practices include the addition of organic material to soil, reduced tillage, and crop and non-crop species diversification (Jezeer et al., 2017).

div.head: Urban
div.p: The restoration and development of natural habitats within urban spaces provides great potential for improving the quality of life in cities, whilst simultaneously contributing to climate change mitigation through carbon sequestration (Seddon et al., 2020). Urban EbA offers several benefits, such as improving drainage systems resulting in reduced flooding, improving air and water quality, and cooling cities (Keelet et al., 2019).

However, EbA faces several challenges and inherent uncertainties (Ojea, 2015). The main challenges associated with EbA include governance structures and participation, measuring effectiveness of adaptation responses, the incorporation of long-term methods for management, witnessing the evidence of tangible results, suitable financial systems, difficulties in implementing EbA, and dealing with the inherent uncertainties associated with climate change (Ojea, 2015;UNEP, 2019;Langsdorf et al., 2022). Reid et al. (2019), highlight similar challenges, including uncertainty about how to finance EbA sustainably and over the long-term, disparities between the enduring effects of climate change and the transient nature of political dynamics, and the scarcity of comprehensive evidence supporting the efficiency and economic feasibility of EbA, and the lack of flexible models and cooperation across sectors and stakeholders. Additionally, EbA, as an intervention in response to climate change impacts, relies on ecological restoration, which in some cases can take many years to provide evidence of physical results (Ojea, 2015). Consequently, it can be uncertain whether EbA provides the necessary benefits at a sufficient rate to provide social-ecological resilience to the rate of climatic change impacts (Ojea, 2015). Evidently, NbS and EbA face similar challenges, three of which are prominent: determining effectiveness of the response, financial viability of the response, and the impact of climate change on the ecosystems and the natural environment that provide adaptation responses.

To summarise, EbA responses have been increasingly touted as effective and cost-efficient alternatives to reducing the impacts of climate change (Ojea, 2015). Evidently, there is increasing recognition of the role that a well-functioning and healthy ecosystem plays in helping society and the environment adapt to climate change impacts (Ojea, 2015). Importantly, EbA places an emphasis on participatory, community-based climate adaptation strategies, which forms part of a broader adaptation strategy that considers multiple social, economic, and environmental benefits for local communities (Langsdorf et al., 2022). However, in addition to challenges of effectiveness, several studies point to difficulties in implementing EbA (Langsdorf et al., 2022).

div.head: Building Resilience to Climate Change Impacts
div.p: When discussing climate change adaptation responses, such as NbS and EbA, there is a growing interest in the concept of resilience, particularly resilience of cities, communities, and the environment to current and projected climate change impacts (Satterthwaite et al., 2020;Folke, 2016). Interestingly, the growth in the concept of resilience is closely linked to the growth in socialecological systems and the idea of an intricately linked social and environmental planet (Folke, 2016).

The increasing interest in resilience is due to the limits associated with traditional climate change adaptation methods (Satterthwaite et al., 2020). For example, when implementing certain climate change adaptation methods, several residual risks remain after all measures have been employed to reduce risks and hazards for vulnerable populations (Satterthwaite et al., 2020). For this reason, increasing attention has been placed on nature-based solutions for climate change adaptation and, more importantly, building social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts.

div.head: Defining resilience
div.p: In the simplest terms, resilience is defined as "the capacity or ability of something, someone, or some group to anticipate, accommodate, cope, adapt, or transform when exposed to specified hazards" (Satterthwaite et al., 2020:144). Put another way, resilience refers to a systems' ability to cope with unexpected shocks and to keep functioning in much the same was as before the shock (Walker, 2020).

Resilience has become popular in development and vulnerability reduction sectors such as disaster risk reduction, community protection and climate change adaptation (Béné et al., 2012). Resilience is frequently discussed through the lens of SESs and is based on the recognition that humans are intimately connected to nature. Recently, the concept of resilience has grown in popularity as the favoured framework for interpreting and responding to climate change complexities (Davidson et al., 2016;Satterthwaite et al., 2020). Borie et al. (2019) agrees that there is increasing hope placed in the ability of resilience thinking to reduce the risks associated with climate change impacts in socialecological systems. To understand resilience, Branco and Waldman (2016) argue that we need to understand how social and ecological systems interact. In the context of social-ecological resilience theory, systems of humans and nature are thought of as constantly changing, highly unpredictable and non-linear phenomena (Nelson, 2011;Folke, 2016;Khan et al., 2020). Subsequently, socialecological resilience theory is increasingly argued to be a suitable approach for managing future climate uncertainties (Khan et al., 2020).

div.head: Defining social-ecological resilience
div.p: Social-ecological resilience refers to the capacity of a system to "anticipate, respond, adapt, or transform in response to shocks, uncertainty, and change, especially novel systemic changes, in order to facilitate desired outcomes" (Biggs et al., 2021:3). In other words, systems that are considered

div.head: Exploring transformative adaptation responses
div.p: Transformative adaptation options become more important as climatic and non-climatic drivers force social and ecological systems to their tipping points (UNEP, 2019). For example, increasing temperatures have caused a shift in the timing of seasonal changes, as well as shifting climatic zones.

As a result, many traditional crops will no longer be viable in certain regions (UNEP, 2019). Due to these changes, the entire local economy could adopt a new model to build resilience to climate change impacts, resulting in socio-economic transformation. It is important to highlight that not all systems need to be changed or altered to build resilience to climate change impacts. If a social-ecological system is evaluated as being able to endure in the face of climate change impacts with sustained provision of ecosystem services, adaptation responses can focus on enhancing the strengths of the system and protecting the ecosystem functioning, thus improving livelihoods within the existing social-ecological context (UNEP, 2019). In this context, adaptation becomes the process of managing existing resilience rather than building resilience. This is achieved by maintaining the existing functions of the system without compromising the future adaptation potential of the system (UNEP, 2019).

div.head: Reducing vulnerability to climate change impacts
div.p: In the context of pressing socio-economic development needs and threatened ecosystem services, South Africa urgently requires adaptive responses to reduce vulnerability to current and future climate change impacts (Ziervogel et al., 2014). It has become increasing apparent that delays in responding to climate change impacts has compromised societies, livelihoods, and well-being in South Africa (Chersich & Wright, 2019). Due to slow progress with mitigation efforts, especially within the energy sector, and corresponding negative attention, South Africa has experienced a shift in focus to developing plans and systems for adaptation to climate change impacts (Chersich & Wright, 2019).

Adaptation measures span a wide array of actions, ranging from bolstering societal and healthcare system resilience to preparing for the ramifications of extreme weather events and mitigating the impacts of rising workplace temperatures (Chersich & Wright, 2019). Importantly, the effectiveness of adaptation responses depends on reducing the country's poverty and inequality levels, particularly amongst women and other vulnerable groups, such as those living in informal settlements (Chersich & Wright, 2019). This links us back to the theory of resilience, simply, if a household's socioeconomic position is strong, they have an increased ability to withstand climate change impacts.

However, a significant number of South Africans are unemployed and over half live below the poverty line, reducing a large portion of the population's resilience to climate change impacts (Chersich & Wright, 2019).

div.head: Climate Change Impacts on the Mining Sector
div.p: The mining sector is particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016;Ndlovu, 2018;Martinez & Davy, 2019). Climate change can have a direct impact on operations and performance, as well as an indirect impact on supply chains and rising energy costs (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016;Martinez & Davy, 2019;ICMM, 2019). Examples of climate change induced risks within the mining sector include water-related impacts (droughts, floods, and storms), heat-related impacts (fires and heat stroke), and sea-level rise in some cases (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). The

Physical climate-related risks can disrupt operations, production, and the financial, social, and environmental performance of the mining sector over time (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Key areas of concern for mining sector management includes water availability, tailings storage facilities, and how climate change may impact mine closure and post-closure, due to their inherent risks and complexities (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Unmanaged climate-related risks threaten mining companies' balance sheet, reputation, their social license to operate, as well as social-ecological systems post-closure (Martinez & Davy, 2019).

Increasingly, we are seeing evidence of climate impacts interacting with other risks that inflict the mining sector, resulting in new, more complex risks to mining operations (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). Climate risks and the failure to adopt industry-wide adaptation approaches to climate change impacts may jeopardise investor confidence and impact social-ecological dynamics over the longterm (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). Although the impacts of extreme weather events experienced in leading mining regions has led to increased attention to sector vulnerabilities, sensitivities and climate change risks, little research and debate has emerged that comprehensively unpacks the links between climate change impacts and the effects on mining operations, the extractives sector, and socialecological systems post-closure (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016).
Climate change impacts that affect water quality and availability is one of the most pressing challenges for the mining sector, both during operations and post-closure (Martinez & Davy, 2019).

Climate change can cause prolonged droughts, leading to increased demands for water conservation by the mine, as well as an increase in the cost of water (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). Prolonged droughts can also lead to conflict with other water users in the region over water availability (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). This becomes particularly challenging if other water users include local communities, which can lead to hostility amongst communities and mining companies (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016). Consequently, it is important for mining companies to mainstream climate risk considerations into existing activities, across the entire project life cycle (Martinez & Davy, 2019).

In my opinion, these considerations should also be accounted for in the planning, design and implementation of mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. In line with Martinez and Davy's findings (2019), there are multiple opportunities available for the integration of climate risk considerations across different stages of the project life cycle. This incorporation can span various aspects, including studies, plans, strategies, and governance processes, ranging from planning and operations to maintenance and decommissioning.

A study conducted by the International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) amongst its members and other key mining sector experts, highlighted several key themes related to a changing climate and how this could impact the mining sector (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Themes relevant to this research are discussed below.

• ICMM member companies have reported experiencing an increase in extreme weather and climate-related risks, affecting mining operations and surrounding communities. Climate impacts have led to a reduction or shutdown of operations, increased capital expenditure, threatened the health and safety of on-site employees, and made vulnerable communities prone to social unrest (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Evidence suggests that future climate change impacts will likely exacerbate these risks (Langsdorf et al., 2022). Hence, it is important for mining companies to consider projected climatic changes when planning mine closure and rehabilitation strategies.

• Declining water availability caused by climate change is a major concern for the mining sector (Martinez & Davy, 2019). The potential consequences of declining water availability include operational challenges, restrictions on water abstraction and consumption, increased water quality regulations, increased water costs, and increased public scrutiny of the mining sector's water consumption practices (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Increased competition for water can lead to social and political conflicts, posing major challenges to business continuity and postclosure social-ecological resilience (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016).

• In some cases, excess water poses a growing risk to mining operations and closure plans (Martinez & Davy, 2019). As emphasized by Martinez and Davy (2019), it is becoming increasingly crucial for mining companies to guarantee the adaptability of tailing dams, water management systems, and waste rock storage facilities in the face of a shifting climate. This necessity pertains to both the operational phase and the post-closure period.

• Importantly in the context of this research, is the recognition that mine closure and postclosure are key areas of climate risk (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Interestingly, the ICMM's research uncovered that its members generally recognise the necessity of incorporating climate change impacts into closure planning, infrastructure decommissioning, and land rehabilitation. However, this practice is presently limited to a minority of ICMM member companies (Martinez & Davy, 2019). In addition, little evidence exists on whether current practice in this regard has been successful. As such, this research could play a role in furthering awareness of planning for climate change impacts during closure and rehabilitation. Martinez and Davy (2019) argue that climate change impacts pose a challenge to mine closure because rehabilitated land will be exposed to warmer temperatures and increased variability in extreme weather events.

• Another interesting theme relevant to this research is the recognition to include host communities in climate risk and social-ecological resilience engagements (Martinez & Davy, 2019). ICMM member companies are becoming increasingly aware of the need to adopt an integrated, multi-stakeholder approach to climate resilience planning, which can benefit mining companies themselves, as well as other stakeholders in the mine's vicinity (Martinez & Davy, 2019). Evidence suggests that partnering with a range of stakeholders, including governments, other private companies, and local communities, can be effective in identifying and implementing climate adaptation responses with shared benefits (Martinez & Davy, 2019).

div.head: Linking Mine Closure and Climate Change Adaptation
div.p: Climate change impacts can exacerbate existing social-ecological and economic vulnerabilities in mining regions (Loginova & Batterbury, 2019). Further, evidence suggests that climate change is already affecting the mining industry, as well as surrounding communities and ecosystems, and projected changes to key variables have the potential to impact all aspects of mining in the future (The Mining Association of Canada, 2021). In the face of projected climatic changes, it is imperative that the mining sector adapts to climate change impacts, taking into consideration both the surrounding communities, as well as environments impacted by mining activities (Crawford, 2019).

According to Crawford (2019), investing in climate change adaptation in and around mine sites can assist the mining industry manage climate-related risks. Additionally, these investments can help build the adaptive capacity of surrounding communities, increasing their resilience to climate change impacts (Crawford, 2019).

Crucially, Loginova and Batterbury (2019) advocate that the mining industry should capitalize on the opportunity provided by climate change to collaborate with communities, governments, and other stakeholders affected in adapting to climate change impacts. The inclusion of host communities and mine employees in decision-making about future mining activities is crucial for ensuring inclusive, informed, and sustainable adaptation (Loginova & Batterbury, 2019). One way of ensuring inclusivity and successful adaptation is through climate resilient development (Loginova et al., 2019). Climate resilient development successfully integrates both mitigation and adaptation actions to advance sustainable development (Langsdorf et al., 2022). As such, climate resilient development can be particularly relevant to mine sites, where surrounding environments and ecosystems have been degraded due to mining activities. Through climate resilient development, the mining industry, together with governments, can support local livelihoods, promote the health of surrounding communities, and restore vital ecosystems to help social-ecological systems adapt to climate change impacts long after the mine has closed (Loginova & Batterbury, 2019). Mining with principles, according to the IMCC (2017), means ensuring that operations and surrounding communities are resilient to climate change impacts, as well as committing to incorporating climate change measures, such as adaptation, into policies and strategies. Key activities for mining companies in this regard are to pinpoint opportunities for climate risk, resilience, and adaptation within existing mining activities and across the entire operational life cycle of the mine (Martinez & Davy, 2019). According to the ICMM's Integrated Mine Closure: Good Practice Guide (2019), one area of risk identification that is evolving quickly in the mining industry is the consideration of climate change impacts on closure and long-term rehabilitation planning. Closure planning should consider the impacts of a changing climate (ICMM, 2019), not only on closure design, but also on host communities and the surrounding environment post-closure. As part of this process, mine closure planning and rehabilitation could include climate change adaptation responses to build social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts post-closure.

div.head: Chapter Summary
div.p: As the literature highlights, South Africa has a long history of mine abandonment, with many more mines projected to close in the coming decade (Crous, 2020). This underscores the importance of understanding current mine closure practices and finding ways to enhance them for a sustainable and This study focuses on the mining sector in particular because of South Africa's history of mine abandonment and because the mining sector is particularly vulnerable to climate change impacts (Rüttinger & Sharma, 2016;Ndlovu, 2018;Martinez & Davy, 2019). From this literature review it became evident that much of the literature on "climate change impacts on the mining industry"

focuses on the climate risks mining operations currently face, with a lack of literature and research on the climate impacts after a mine closes. In the face of projected climatic changes, it is imperative that the mining sector adapts to climate change impacts, taking into consideration both the surrounding communities, as well as environments impacted by mining activities (Crawford, 2019).
Chapter 3: Research Methodology

div.head: Introduction
div.p: This chapter outlines the choices that have shaped the approach and execution of this research, along with the methodologies used to gather, sift through, process, and analyse information. I begin by delving into the paradigm and research methodology that underpinned my study. Following that, I describe the data collection methods employed, and subsequently detail the data analysis techniques used. Finally, I address the ethical concerns and methodological constraints inherent to this research.

Given the nature of the intended study, the proposed research approach adheres to a qualitative framework, anchored in a constructivist and interpretivist paradigm. The research methods for data collection consisted of an in-depth literature review, report review, policy scoping, and semistructured/informal interviews. Data was analysed using manual coding techniques.

div.head: Research Paradigm
div.p: A research paradigm is defined as "a cluster of beliefs and dictates which for scientists in a particular

discipline influence what should be studied, how research should be done, [and] how results should be interpreted" (Bryman, 1988:4). Furthermore, a paradigm can be described as "a way of seeing the world that frames a research topic", which in turn influences the way that researchers think about the topic (Hughes, 2010:35). Hughes (2010) argues that all research is underpinned by a paradigm, or by a particular way of viewing and interpreting the world. Importantly, all researchers have their own understanding and interpretation of knowledge, truth, and the world (Chilisa & Kawulich, 2012). In addition to being aware of external factors influencing research, researchers need to be aware of how their own thoughts, beliefs and opinions can influence their research. In terms of conducting qualitative research in particular, the researchers' personal thoughts and beliefs about explored topics will guide the direction of their research.

For my research, I adopted a qualitative research approach to unearth deeper meaning and understanding (Preiser et al., 2022) of my research topic. Opting for a qualitative research approach provides researchers with the means to enhance their understanding of intricate concepts, social interactions, or cultural phenomena. This approach proves particularly advantageous when delving into the exploration of the reasons behind or the mechanisms through which particular events have unfolded, proving useful in the exploration of how or why certain events have occurred, interpreting a variety of social interactions, and describing actions (Bryman et al., 2019). Unlike a quantitative research approach, qualitative research is exploratory and can be used when the researcher does not have a clear idea of the outcome of the study, as was the case with this research process. For example, during the preliminary literature review for this research study, it became evident that literature pertaining to the interconnected nature of mine closure, climate change impacts post-closure and the social-ecological resilience of surrounding areas was limited, and the outcome of the study remained unclear. Thus, adopting a qualitative research approach allowed me to delve deeper into issues of interest, enabling themes to emerge from the gathered data, and delve back into the literature to verify what the emergent themes might mean in the context of existing discourse. Furthermore, a qualitative approach allowed my own reflections and expertise on the topic to guide the direction of my research.

According to Preiser et al. (2022:274), qualitative research's goal is to discover patterns and "produce understanding", enabling a researcher to understand the foundations of related behaviour. In other words, a qualitative research approach adds valuable details to the data and can give a human voice to your findings. This is particularly important when researching and understanding complex adaptive systems, such as the interconnected social-ecological systems surrounding mines in South Africa.

Qualitative research can result in a deeper understanding of a topic and provide more interpretive findings than those produced by a quantitative study. This is important in the context of my research study, where I was exploring several related topics with undefined boundaries and using my work experience to guide the direction of my study. Approaches in qualitative research, like semistructured interviews, are often associated with constructivism and interpretivism, which are aimed at gaining a deeper understanding of "context-dependent variables and realities" (Shackleton et al., 2022:109).

Given that I aimed to explore and gain a deeper understanding of the complexities, nuances, and interdependencies associated with mining companies and the surrounding social-ecological systems, as well as the impacts of climate change on this complex system, I anchored my research in a constructivist and interpretivist ontological and subjective epistemological paradigm. To provide context, constructivism, as an ontological position, argues that social phenomena is continually shaped and influenced by individual and collective social actors through social interactions (Bryman & Bell, 2014). Importantly, constructivism argues that "reality is in a constant state of flux, is subjective and that multiple realities co-exist" (Bryman & Bell, 2014:48). In other words, a constructivist paradigm is not conducted within clearly controlled boundaries and in line with clearly defined variables, nor is the researcher in this instance a neutral party to the studied phenomena.

Rather, the researcher's worldly thoughts, opinions and beliefs play a role in how the research is conducted, how the studied phenomena are interpreted and the direction of the research. Further, the aim of a constructivist approach is to understand a particular situation or phenomena in the context of the researcher's thoughts, opinions, and beliefs on the topic at hand. As such, I undertook my study with the perspective that the opinions of the environmental, social and governance or mine closure specialists who I interviewed are shaped and influenced by a myriad of social actors through the social interactions that they are exposed to in their field of work. In addition, I approached this research process cognisant of the influence of my thoughts, beliefs, and opinions in steering the direction of the study.
Highly subjective studies are closely linked to a constructivist paradigm (Bryman & Bell, 2014).

Thus, in concurrence with the constructivist paradigm, I intended to understand the subjective perceptions of the identified specialists during the interview process. In doing so, this allowed me to unpack the participants' involvement within the bounds of the mining company, knowing that their responses would be based on their subjective reflections from experiences within their roles.

According to both Burrell and Morgan (1979) and Bryman and Bell (2014), the two major assumptions contained within paradigms are objectivism and subjectivism. Briefly defined, objectivism is best suited to studies pertaining to the natural sciences that value-controlled environments, defined variables, and neutrality (Guba & Lincoln, 1994). From an organisational study perspective, objectivism argues that the organisation exists purely because of the structures enabling its existence (Bryman & Bell, 2014).

On the other hand, Burrell and Morgan (1979:102) suggest that subjectivism takes the view that "an organisation is socially constructed by individuals to make sense of their social experience". In other words, the organisation can only be understood if the individual is directly involved in the functioning of that organisation. Subjectivism values the importance of contextual detail, infinite variables and considers the researcher a part of the subject being studied (Guba & Lincoln, 1994). A subjectivist approach is favourable as it highlights the importance of context, infinite variables, and individuals, allowing me to explore beyond clearly defined boundaries, often imposed by a quantitative research design and objective epistemological paradigm. In respect of my research study, it was important for me to provide context to my study, as well as place emphasis on the various social and ecological systems involved in mine closure and rehabilitation practices in South Africa to understand and derive deeper meaning from the findings of this study. Due to the complexity of the studied phenomenon, the subjectivist approach allowed me to consider a wider range of variables, leading to a better understanding of the research topic and the interconnected nature of these variables, such as the social-ecological systems surrounding mines in South Africa, as well as the impact of mine closure on these complex systems.
By adopting a constructivist paradigm, I subjectively engaged with the data I collected from interviews, literature reviews and secondary data analyses, throughout this research process.

Importantly, I recognised that my engagement with the collected data was influenced by my preexisting perceptions, thoughts, values, and beliefs. In line with Charmaz's perspective (2005), as researchers, we actively participate in the construction and interpretation of qualitative data. In other words, our findings are often reflective of our interpretation rather than completely objective.

Therefore, while constructivism serves as a valuable overarching paradigm, I also incorporated an interpretivist paradigm into this research process. This allowed me to center my focus on the meanings, experiences, and interpretations shared by the experts during the interview phase.

Adopting an interpretivist paradigm allowed me to investigate several variables at a greater level of depth, resulting in detailed and meaningful findings, providing me with better insights for further action later. According to Shackleton et al. (2022), interpretivism places an emphasis on the researcher's role as interpreter of collected data and the process of creating knowledge. Interpretivists argue that the studied phenomena of the social sciences (people and organisations) are largely different from the studied phenomena of the natural sciences (Bryman & Bell, 2014). Therefore, interpretivism requires that research approaches are cognisant of the differences between people and their institutions in a social science setting and objects of the natural sciences (Bryman & Bell, 2014).

Interpretivism is closely linked to the subjectivism school of thought, in that social studies cannot be limited to controlled environments and clearly defined variables. Evidently, both interpretivism and subjectivism assert that the study of the social world requires a logic that "reflects the distinctiveness of humans" (Bryman & Bell, 2014:14) and requires the researcher to "grasp the subjective meaning of social action" (Bryman & Bell, 2014:14). Interpretivist paradigms are suitable to qualitative research studies, as is the case with my research study.

div.head: Research Approach
div.p: I shaped my study using an inductive research approach to facilitate my data collection and analysis process. According to Guba and Lincoln (1994), a research approach informs how researchers collect knowledge. My research approach guided me in determining what data I decided to collect, and how I collated and analysed the data. As already mentioned, my research study was based on a qualitative research methodology, which is closely aligned with a constructivist and interpretivist ontological paradigm. The following table details how I conducted my research based on the aim and objectives of my study. The table relates my research objectives, data collection choices, the type of data I collected to achieve the research objectives, and the desired findings of the research collection method.

div.head: Research Methods
div.p: According to Bryman and Bell (2014) Multi-method approaches are becoming increasingly popular, particularly when considering the complexities associated with social-ecological systems (de Vos et al., 2022). A multi-method approach is therefore useful for understanding the complexities associated with the social-ecological resilience of mines in South Africa. Collecting data from multiple and varied sources ensures a broad and comprehensive understanding of a studied phenomenon. According to de Vos et al. (2022:52), a multi-method approach can be employed "with a view to understanding different aspects of the system rather than understanding the same process or dynamic from a complementary perspective".
A multi-method approach was particularly important for this research study due to my preconceived opinions and biases on mine closure, climate change adaptation, and social-ecological resilience.

Exploring multiple sources of data ensured that I limited my bias, and consistently broadened my Consistent with a qualitative research approach, my last data collection method comprised conducting semi-structured interviews with environmental, social and governance experts employed at mining companies in South Africa. Interviews ensured that my research findings provided real-life context and valuable insight from experts actively involved in the mine closure space. Shackleton et al. (2022) argues that when unpacking the intricacies linked with social-ecological systems, expert knowledge about the system is important for guiding your interpretation of the results and findings of your research study. The interview process helped me to achieve the second objective of this research process, which was to determine the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation. Throughout this process, my literature review evolved, influenced by the data I collected and as new findings and insights emerged. The following section details the research methods I used for this research.

div.head: Conducting a Literature Review
div.p: In line with a qualitative research approach, I began my study with a preliminary review of relevant literature, which progressed into an extensive literature review as I proceeded with the research study.

Although not originally intended, I refined and adjusted my literature review as new and relevant nuances and reflections emerged as the data collection and semi-structured interview process progressed. As a result, my literature review became an iterative process. However, the main themes of my literature remained constant throughout the process. Whilst a literature review is argued as a method for identifying gaps in the literature and not a research method for collecting data, I included it here as the information gathered during the literature review informed, to some extent, the findings of my research study. During the research process, I read academic, peer-reviewed literature (including journals and books), as well as grey literature, such as the IPCC reports. In addition, I also included some of the less cited work, which I found to be more valuable in some cases by offering different perspectives, especially on controversial issues such as mine closure in South Africa.

div.head: Data Collection
div.p: In addition to conducting a literature review, I collected qualitative data for analysis through semistructured interviews, as well as through a review of relevant mining reports and the regulations pertaining to mine closure and rehabilitation in South Africa. As such my data collection methods involved 'interviewing' and 'collecting' (Yin, 2011). It is important to highlight that whilst the data collected from the participants remains anonymous, the information collected from company reports was extracted from publicly available documents and is accessible to anyone interested in reviewing these reports. As such, the results section refers to anonymous participants but references the relevant mining company report where applicable. It is also important to note that the interview participants and selected mining companies are not connected in any way; not all mines have publicly available reports, and not all mines included in the report analysis participated in interviews. Hence, it is possible to name the mining company where publicly available information from reports was used, whilst maintaining the anonymity of the participants. The process of selecting mines is discussed further in the next section.

div.head: Report Review
div.p: To develop an understanding of current best practice amongst mining companies, I identified several mining companies and conducted a review of their integrated annual or sustainability reports to extract information pertaining to their mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. Mining companies usually include a high-level overview of their closure and rehabilitation plans in their publicly available integrated annual or sustainability reports since mine closure strategy documents are not required to be made publicly available by current regulations. Consequently, I unpacked information contained within publicly available mining company documents, such as integrated annual or sustainability reports if available. The method for identification of the mining companies, as well as the information extracted from the reports, is detailed in the subsequent section. Objective one of this research study was to identify examples of mine closure strategies in South Africa that already incorporate climate change adaptation. The benchmark to evaluate this objective was to determine if the strategy mentioned climate change adaptation or whether they implemented rehabilitation activities that contribute to climate change adaptation. Hence, it was important for me to understand what mining companies are currently reporting on with respect to closure and rehabilitation. In addition, I also reviewed mainstream reports (i.e., publicly available documents such as the ICMM best practice guidelines on mine closure, the International Gold Standard Principles (IGSP), and Anglo American's Toolkit on responsible mine closure) for cross-checking information collected later during the interview process. In hindsight, this step in the research method process assisted in providing context in preparation for the interview stage. The method I followed for this data collection process is detailed below.

div.head: Selecting mines to review
div.p: To collect the data for this stage of the research study, I identified the four largest mining sectors by production output in South Africa using a Google search (i.e., coal, platinum, gold, and iron ore).

Across the four largest sectors, I identified the four biggest mines relevant to each sector based on annual production (i.e., four mines and their associated mining companies), and then conducted an in-depth analysis of these mining companies' publicly available Integrated Annual Reports (IAR) or
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Reports or Sustainability Reports. Identifying the mining companies in this manner prevented bias in my selection of participating mining companies.
Additionally, I selected the largest mining companies for review, as industry leaders often have the most extensive reporting available.

After the selection of the four participating mining companies, I identified nine key words (see Table 3) related to my research study to extract relevant information from the identified mining company reports. I then downloaded each of the companies' publicly available reports and conducted a search of each of the key words across all four mining companies to ensure consistency. Whilst some of the mining companies only had annual integrated reports, a few of the mining companies also had ESG or sustainability reports. As such, my first port of call was an ESG or sustainability report. If the company had neither, I extracted information from their integrated annual report using the same nine key words. I set up an excel spreadsheet for capturing the data and then extracted all relevant information pertaining to each key word across all four companies and inserted this information into my spreadsheet for analysis. It was important for me to use the same nine key words across all four companies to ensure consistency. Importantly, I had to ensure that the information I extracted was related to mine closure and rehabilitation practices and not part of the companies' broader environmental strategy. The extracted information was analysed and used to inform my research findings, which is detailed in the subsequent chapter. The key words were selected based on the objectives of this research study and relevance to the subject matter.

div.p: Climate Change Climate change refers to the ongoing shift in Earth's weather patterns and temperatures. This leads to various environmental and societal impacts, such as extreme weather events and rising sea levels (UNFCCC, 2021).

div.head: Mine closure
div.p: Mine closure refers to the process undertaken when the operational stage of a mine comes to an end, or has ended, and final decommissioning and mine rehabilitation is underway (Grant et al., 2016).

div.head: Rehabilitation
div.p: Mine rehabilitation refers to the restoration of the post-mined landscape to the intended post-mining land use (Grant et al., 2016).

div.head: Biodiversity
div.p: Biodiversity refers to all life on earth, encompassing all living organisms, from tiny microorganisms to large animals and plants (National Geographic Society, 2023).

div.head: Social/Communities
div.p: A community is a group of individuals living in the same area and interacting with each other (MacQueen et al., 2001).

Nature-based solutions Nature-based Solutions encompass strategies aimed at safeguarding, responsibly overseeing, and revitalizing both unaltered and altered ecosystems. These approaches adeptly and flexibly tackle societal dilemmas while concurrently promoting mutual advantages for both human communities and the environment (The World Bank, 2022).

div.head: Ecosystems
div.p: Ecosystems are complex networks of living organisms and their surroundings, working together in a delicate balance to support life and provide essential services for the environment and society (National Geographic Society, 2023).

div.head: Just transition
div.p: The just transition refers to the process of moving the country's economy from heavily reliant industries, such as mining and fossil fuels, to more environmentally sustainable sectors. This transition aims to minimize negative impacts on workers and communities dependent on these industries, ensuring they have opportunities for retraining and new employment in green sectors (World Resources Institute, 2022).

div.head: Policy Scoping
div.p: According to Biggs et al. (2022), when your research topic involves social-ecological systems, as is the case with my research study, it is important to identify and review relevant policies or regulations that can affect the social-ecological system under consideration. In line with this reasoning, I conducted a review of the relevant regulations that govern mine closure and rehabilitation in South Africa as a supportive data collection method. This ensured that I developed a sound understanding of the regulations that affect the social-ecological systems that form part of my research study; in other words, the communities and environments that surround mines in South Africa and encouraged me to consider the wider complexities associated with mine closure and rehabilitation. In addition to this reasoning, a review of the relevant regulations was a helpful method for crosschecking insights collected during the interview stage of this research study. Additionally, it was important for me to gain an understanding of the boundaries within which mine closure must occur as regulated by the relevant legislation, as well as to determine whether climate change adaptation is, or can be, incorporated into the current regulations. This would ultimately influence the findings of this research study.

The main law currently governing mine closure in South Africa is the National Environmental Management Act (NEMA), and the 2015 Financial Provisioning Regulations published in terms of NEMA, read together with the Environmental Impact Assessment Regulations, and the Minerals and Petroleum Resources Development Act. The first step in this data collection method involved desktop based research, to provide context for myself in terms of the relevant regulations. This involved gathering information regarding the current regulations, as well as the history of the changes to these regulations and changes to the law governing mine closure in South Africa, as well as the reasons for these changes. During this process, I also took note of the positive aspects of the changes, as well as some of the associated negative changes or remaining challenges perceived by the mining industry.

div.head: Semi-structured Interviews
div.p: Recognising that I needed to collect qualitative, open-ended data, I chose to conduct semi-structured interviews. This is in alignment with Bryman et al. (2019:23), who point out that semi-structured interviews allow the researcher to "keep an open mind", allowing concepts and theories to develop out of the interview process. In addition to this reasoning, my decision to use semi-structured interviews is further supported by Shackleton et al. (2022), who suggests that in certain socialecological research studies, an informal approach to the interview process may be beneficial, as often opportunities for collecting data and related insights arise unexpectedly. Due to the sensitivities around mine closure and the impact on communities and the surrounding environment, it was important for me to develop trust and make participants feel comfortable to share meaningful insights, which can often be achieved through the more casual nature of a semi-structured interview (Shackleton et al., 2022). Lastly, semi-structured interviews also allowed me to delve more deeply into sensitive topics, providing valuable insight for developing my research findings. Through the interview process, I aimed to address the second objective of this research: determining the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure plans in South Africa, for both the mining company and the surrounding community and environment. As a result, I formulated my interview questions to gather the essential data needed to comprehend and achieve this objective.

I initiated the interview phase of this research by utilising a preliminary set of proposed questions instead of a rigid, fully scripted questionnaire. This approach provided me with the flexibility to adapt my inquiries based on participants' responses, fostering more spontaneous and candid conversations while also eliciting valuable insights. My intention was to probe the participant but not limit their response and allowing the interview to go in any direction, as aligned with a qualitative research approach. Additionally, I wanted leeway to ask further questions in response to replies that I deemed significant (Bryman, et al., 2019). Importantly, I included open-ended questions in my interviews to avoid participants limiting their replies to a single-word response, ensuring that I collected deeper and more valuable data. Due to the complexities and nuances associated with this research topic, it was not only important that I collected data from experts in the field, but also that the data that was collected allowed me to understand contextual conditions and relevant trends, which would not have been possible to achieve through a structured interview. A sample interview guide can be found in Appendix A. Given the constraints on time, I opted to keep my sample size limited to 8 participants.

This decision aligns with the approach suggested by Miles et al. (2014), wherein qualitative participant sampling often involves a focus on smaller samples chosen for the contextual relevance they bring to the study.

During the initial phases of my research study, I adopted a purposive sampling method to select interview participants for data collection. Purposive sampling refers to the selection of participants with direct reference to your research aim or objectives (Bryman et al., 2019). As Yin (2011) points out, the goal of sampling in this manner is to identify participants who will yield the most relevant and plentiful data. I used this sampling approach initially as I had already met and made several key contacts within the mining industry that were relevant to my research aim and objectives. In line with my research aim and objectives, I focused on contacting a selection of experts within the environmental, social and governance (ESG) divisions of mining companies in South Africa, due to their exposure to developing, implementing, and reviewing mine closure and rehabilitation strategies.

My research participants were South Africans and experts either in ESG or mine closure and rehabilitation. I identified several participants from a range of prominent mining companies in South Africa to engage with and interview.
In line with a purposive sampling approach, my criteria for participant selection included the following:
• Individuals with direct involvement in mine closure and rehabilitation planning either through development, planning or execution.

• Experts were not limited to ESG divisions, anyone involved in mine closure and rehabilitation could be recruited as a participant as such individuals could provide valuable alternative insights (this is because mine closures are not limited to ESG divisions as there are several aspects of mine closures to consider).

In support of Yin's (2011:303) advice to include "sources that might offer contradictory evidence or views" when utilising a purposive sampling approach, I purposefully selected a broad range of participants from a variety of mining companies, in the hope that they might have different perspectives, limiting any possibility of confirming my own preconceptions and adding an interesting dynamic to my research findings. After the initial purposive sampling approach, I then proceeded with snowball sampling, which involved initiating contact with initially identified participants and using these connections to further expand my sample size by establishing new contacts. Snowball sampling was incredibly useful for collecting the data required for this research study, as often a participant that I was interviewing would know of someone else who could be interviewed. This also allowed for diversity in my research participants and collected data.

Once prospective participants agreed to participate, I organised a date and time suitable for them and sent a Microsoft Team's meeting invite for the agreed upon date and time. All interviews were conducted via Microsoft Teams on my private Stellenbosch University Teams channel and lasted between one to one and a half hours. Each interview, with the permission of the participant, was recorded and transcribed using Microsoft Team's recording and transcription function.
