Importantly, thematic coding is a qualitative analysis method that entails identifying text passages connected by a shared theme. This allows for the categorisation of text and the creation of a "framework of thematic ideas" about it (Gibbs, 2007:62). As such, coding helped me conceptualise underlying themes derived from the interview process to conceptualise what is occurring within this space (Bryant & Charmaz, 2007) and, therefore, give significance to the data I acquired through the interview process. Coding helped in linking relevant data to my three research objectives, as well as develop sub-headings in order to explore each objective in more detail. I made use of an iterative coding process broken up into several steps as described below (Bryman & Bell, 2014):

• The first step directly after an interview was to process the raw data for further analysis. This included taking down during the interview and noting interesting insights or my "after interview thoughts" directly after each interview. Already at this stage, I began grouping my thoughts under different sub-headings, as well as adding my own questions and thinking to these notes. All interviews were transcribed automatically by MS Teams during the interview.

• After all the interviews were conducted, I broke each of the three objectives down into the remained open to altering my interpretation of the emerging themes. I found this approach effective, especially for maintaining a dynamic perspective throughout the coding process.
• After this initial post-it notes coding phase, I conducted an initial read-through of the interview transcripts without taking any notes.

• I then proceeded to read through the transcripts again, this time highlighting key statements using different colours for different topics (for example, statements relating to climate change adaptation were highlighted in green) and making detailed notes for each interview. At this stage I began developing initial codes, by identifying themes in the interview response. These themes or codes would eventually guide the development of sub-headings for the in-depth analysis and exploration of each of the three objectives. During this phase of the coding process, I also began extracting relevant and key quotes from the transcriptions and plotted these quotes under the relevant emerging themes.

• After the second round of reading, I proceeded to further unpack my codes while also embarking on the process of generating overarching theoretical concepts in conjunction with the amassed data. Employing coding as a method, I systematically organized similar data segments into coherent themes and sub-themes, each correspondingly aligned with one of the three research objectives. Themes here refer to features of a participant's account characterising perceptions and/or experiences that I, as the researcher, saw as relevant to my research objectives. This process transformed a large quantity of unstructured data into structured and categorised data, creating a blueprint for me to draw further conclusions for my research findings. I used this process to develop the sub-headings for each research objective.

• I assigned more than one code to one section of data, and I limited the number of codes I generated to my area of interest. Limiting the number of codes ensured that my collected data remained relevant to the objective I was attempting to unpack through this process.
• Lastly, I plotted the relevant data collected and the quotes extracted from the interviews to the identified sub-headings of each of the three research objectives.

div.head: Thematic Analysis
div.p: Thematic analysis is regarded as one of the prevalent methods for qualitative data analysis (Bryman et al., 2019). Since I had already used certain key words to collect the data from mining reports and mine closure regulations, I utilised a thematic analysis approach to examine the data gathered through these research methods. As with coding, thematic analysis identifies themes or patterns in the collected data (Preiser et al., 2022). I used thematic analysis inductively. Preiser et al. (2022) suggests that when adopting thematic analysis as a data analysis tool, researchers can choose themes based on their capacity to address a research question or fulfill a research objective. As such, I identified themes relevant to the three objectives of this research study. My theme identification process was guided by Preiser et al. (2022:274) suggested three stages for identifying themes for thematic analysis:
• I began the process with an initial and holistic reading of the mining reports and mine closure regulations.

• I then fragmented the text by identifying key and relevant subsections (this was guided by my prior reading and research objectives). This was followed by coding the identified subsections. The themes I selected were guided by the key words I used to extract the information during the data collection phase.
• Lastly, I elaborated and refined the emerging themes as I progressed through more text.

I then plotted the relevant information obtained during the report review and policy scoping phase to the sub-headings I identified during the coding phase to support or contradict information collected during the semi-structured interviews. I used different colours to keep track of how the information was collected (for example, regulatory information was indicated as red text). As a last step in the thematic analysis process, I returned to the literature and extracted key points from the literature review and plotted these to the sub-headings. After completing the final data analysis, I proceeded to provide a concise overview of my findings, along with offering recommendations for potential future research within the field.

div.head: Ethical Considerations
div.p: Ethical considerations are an important aspect of any research process. I reached out via introductory emails to people who either met the criteria for inclusion in my study or knew of someone who met the criteria for inclusion (in other words-snowball sampling). In the email, I briefly detailed the aim of my thesis and listed some of the key topics that will be covered in the interview and asked whether they would be interested in participating. Although the research process covered topics that I have worked on at my place of employment, there was no conflict of interest as I did not use specific information obtained from clients. I also requested and obtained permission from my current employer to conduct this research, as well as conduct interviews pertaining to my research topic. At the start of each interview, I briefly explained the aims and objectives of my research and the intended purpose of the interview to the participant to ensure transparency. I also made it clear that all interviewees and associated companies will be completely anonymous, with no identifying factors described in my thesis or note taking. Importantly, I emphasised that the interview process was about collecting information about the expert's opinions of the mining industry as a whole and was not intended to be reflective of the mining company for which they work. Following the explanation of my research's goals and objectives, I sought consent to record and transcribe the interview, ensuring the participant that confidentiality would be maintained.

Additionally, throughout the course of this research process, I strived to ensure that no harm was inflicted on participants and their organisations during the interview process, nor during any other interactions of a similar nature. Furthermore, I ensured that I maintained the anonymity and confidentiality of participants for the duration of the research process to avoid inflicting harm.

Importantly, each of my interview participants either filled out a consent form (see Appendix C) or gave verbal confirmation of their willingness to participate in my research prior to commencement of the interviews. I also took care to ensure that individuals and organisations involved cannot be identified, which is also in line with the Protection of Personal Information Act. Only the organisational sector and participant's role in the organisation was disclosed during this research (i.e., Head of Sustainability -Gold mine). Any documents that participants provided that are not publicly available, remained confidential. Participants were fully informed of the research topic and aim, and of how I intended to utilise the information obtained from the interview process. Lastly, participants were free to withdraw consent or discontinue participation at any time if they no longer felt comfortable to continue with the interview process. According to Preiser et al. (2022), completely removing the subjectivity of a lived experience is not possible, hence it is important for a researcher to adopt a critical and reflective lens for identifying and managing biases, particularly when interpreting a participant's lived experience during the interview process. Considering the above, it was important for me to collate my data in a considered and selective manner, as free from bias as possible. While the constructionist foundation of my research approach acknowledges that complete neutrality in data interpretation is unattainable, I endeavored to maintain objectivity by structuring my interviews to prioritize listening and observation over sharing and prompting.

In addition to the limitations associated with bias, two other aspects of this research process presented limitations. The first limitation was associated with the data analyses aspect of this research study. It is my opinion that the data analyse was limited since I could not access actual mine closure and rehabilitation plans, but rather had to rely on information extrapolated from closure plans and presented in company reports, such as Integrated Annual Reports and Sustainability Reports.

Although these reports provide a lot of information pertaining to mine closure and rehabilitation strategies, I think it would have been beneficial for the purpose of this research study to review and unpack in detail the contents of a mine closure plan, as well as compare plans from several mines to develop an understanding of what is common practice. However, as was indicated to me during the interview process, in their current state mine closure plans are merely "tick-box" exercises that were written many years ago to comply with South African regulations at the time. This practice should change going forward as new, more detailed regulations come into effect.

div.head: How Best Practice Influences Mine Closure Strategies
div.p: Early in my investigations, it became evident that there has been a significant evolution in the way that mining companies approach mine closure and rehabilitation in recent years. Importantly, participants spoke of how the industry as a whole is starting to consider the long-term impacts of their rehabilitation activities. For example, mining companies are starting to use the following statements in their annual reporting: "striving for our mines to leave a positive, healthy and sustainable legacy" (Anglo American Sustainability Report, 2021:21). This is further portrayed by the uptake in to look at how they operate, and closure forms a part of that. This opinion was supported by participant 001 who highlighted that "Mining isn't sustainable, but how do we mine sustainably?".

On the other hand, however, my findings also highlighted that although there is an increased focus on the long-term impacts of rehabilitation activities within the mining industry in South Africa, unfortunately there are several factors unique to South Africa that limit mining companies' ability to achieve successful rehabilitation. One of these challenges was clearly highlighted by participant 002:

"More and more government is relying on mines to partner with them and do everything in terms of service delivery." This, unfortunately, means that current best practice for mining companies in South Africa is often service delivery. This influences mine closure strategies, as often mining companies' resources are diverted to service delivery in an area and not focused on funding long-term and impactful rehabilitation activities as part of their closure strategies. Furthermore, this form of best practice can also have a devasting impact on doorstep communities' post-closure, for once the mine ceases operations and moves away, basic service delivery also ceases. The literature highlights that the issue arises post-closure when the local municipality is responsible for service delivery once more but no longer has the capacity to do so (Edwards & Maritz, 2019). This makes surrounding communities and mining towns particularly vulnerable to external shocks, such as climate change, when the mine is no longer there.

In alignment with this, participants detailed the challenges they face in South Africa. Because infrastructure and basic service delivery in South Africa is not good, mining companies have had to use funds to fix infrastructure or provide services instead of using these funds to support local communities grow their businesses for example. The findings clearly highlighted that, unfortunately, Another negative practice that influences mine closure strategies in South Africa, is the "on-selling" of mines about to reach operational closure. Selling mines on as a liability is a big issue in South Africa, as smaller mining companies will buy the mine, mine the remaining minerals, and then they do not have the funds for effective closure. Abandoned mines result in a significant source of environmental and social problems in South Africa. According to Perkins et al. (2020), mine closure and rehabilitation responsibilities are commonly avoided in South Africa through this process of "onselling". Whilst this is not considered "best practice", alarmingly, it seems to be the most common practice in South Africa as highlighted by both participants and the literature on closure in South Africa. Participant 005 made this case by suggesting that "Industrial mines tend to try and not close mines. When it gets to the point where there's only, let's say, three years of mining left, they try and sell it (the mine) off to people that are less environmentally responsible or don't have the financial capacity to close successfully." This is mainly because closure is costly and complicated.

Anglo American's Mine Closure Toolbox (2019:3) highlights, for example, that "the sale of mines to junior operators is often an alternative to closure implementation, particularly where the junior (operators) may be able to extend the life of the asset." In this sense, it almost seems as though onselling is put forward as a viable alternative to closure in line with current best practice. Anglo American's Toolbox (2019:3) continues by saying that "Regardless of whether disposal is an option, good closure planning and concurrent rehabilitation will add value to the asset." In my opinion, it seems that the first prize for mining companies, or "best practice", is selling the mine to junior operators, whilst the second prize is planning for successful mine closure and rehabilitation. This is further supported by the fact that South Africa has an extensive history of mismanaging mine closure, as highlighted in the literature by Perkins et al. (2020). As a result, South African can boast very few examples of successful closure to date (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020).

On a more positive note, my review of mine closure best practice also revealed an increased focus on climate change considerations. For example, one of the requirements of the ICMM's Closure Maturity Framework ( 2022) is for mining companies to take climate change into account in closure planning. This is closely aligned to the ICMM's Integrated Mine Closure: Good Practice Guide (2019:36) which highlights that "one of the areas of risk where practice is evolving rapidly is the consideration of climate change impacts on closure and long-term planning." The reason for the rapid evolution in practice is the increased recognition that mine closure and post-closure are key areas of climate risk, as detailed in the literature by Martinez and Davy, (2019). Interestingly, a study conducted by the ICMM found that most of its members are generally aware of the need for climate change impacts to be considered as part of closure planning and land rehabilitation, however, this is currently only happening at a small number of ICMM member companies (Haworth, Hamaker-Taylor & Connell, 2019). Little evidence exists on whether current practice in this regard has been successful. When asked about incorporating climate change considerations in mine closure planning, multiple participants indicated that this should be a consideration; however, not a single participant could describe how this could be incorporated. Further, not one of the mining companies represented by the participants was currently considering climate change impacts or adaptation as part of their closure and rehabilitation strategies that they knew of. Even though the ICMM Integrated Mine Closure Guide (2019:101) suggests that "Closure planning should consider the impacts of a changing climate on closure design", because "climate change can affect many aspects of closure design".

This highlights the discrepancy between the guidance provided by best practice and what is being implemented by mining companies who claim to be aligned with best practice. Based on this gap, the following section unpacks the role that the regulations can play in enforcing sustainable and effective closure and rehabilitation practices in South Africa.

div.head: The Role of the Regulations in Sustainable Mine Closure
div.p: My findings from the previous section clearly highlight that best practice guidelines do not necessarily drive change (particularly in countries that are not well-regulated). Although larger mining companies are known to "on-sell" their closure liability, this practice is especially true for the smaller mining companies, who are likely not to go above and beyond what is required of them from a regulatory perspective. Currently, the literature suggests that closure best practice is not challenging or changing industry practice sufficiently to achieve effective mine closure and rehabilitation in South Africa. Hence, the need for well-established, clear, and implementable regulations that effectively govern closure and rehabilitation. This is particularly true when considering alternative methods of closure and rehabilitation, such as incorporating climate change adaptation into closure strategies, because companies will not necessarily adopt this requirement unless it forms part of the countryspecific regulations governing closure.

According to the literature, and supported by several participants, the latest regulations have prompted mining companies to rethink how to effectively plan for closure. Key changes to the regulations are explored in depth in section 2.2.1. However, the most significant change, in my opinion, is the introduction of the idea of restoring the mined site to its pre-mining condition. As outlined by Edwards & Maritz (2019), South African mining companies are legally obligated to engage in closure activities at the conclusion of a mine's operational lifespan. These activities aim to establish post-closure land purposes that find approval not only from the mine itself but also from neighboring communities and stakeholders who are affected either directly or indirectly. Whilst the guidelines for what the "pre-mining condition" might look like has changed over the years, I believe that this was a positive turning point in the regulations. This requirement meant that mining companies could no longer abandon mines without any consequences. The mining company now had to achieve some level of rehabilitation in order to secure a closure certificate. Another important change brought about by the introduction of the 2015 Financial Provisioning Regulations is that the regulations now require mine owners to make financial provisions for all environmental responsibilities related to the mine. This means that mining companies are required to financially prepare for closure and rehabilitation, ensuring that the mining company has the funds available for rehabilitation when operations come to an end. Both of these changes to the regulations have Stellenbosch University https://scholar.sun.ac.za

While the 2015 Financial Provisioning Regulations are an upgrade on the past regulations, the main improvement being the introduction of financial provisioning for closure, the mining industry still grapples with several challenges. One improvement highlighted by several of the participants is the requirement for regular reviews of the financial provisions. These reviews ensure that the amount set aside remains relevant and adequate based on changing circumstances, such as inflation, increased rehabilitation costs, or changes in the scope of operations. Another important improvement highlighted by the participants is the need to ring-fence the funds set aside for environmental rehabilitation, meaning they are kept separate from the company's operational funds. This prevents the misuse of these funds for other purposes. Additionally, the 2015 Financial Provisioning

Regulations established penalties for non-compliance, which can include fines and potential suspension or cessation of operations. This creates an incentive for companies to abide by the financial provisioning requirements. Lastly, the participants also highlighted that the regulations now encourage public participation in the process of determining financial provisioning requirements.
This promotes transparency and accountability in environmental management.

On the other hand, several of the participants highlighted that the current regulations remain onerous and over-regulate the industry. Throughout my interviews, almost all my participants mentioned the need for a shift in the current regulatory environment in South Africa due to the following challenges associated with the current Financial Provisioning Regulations:

• The mining industry feels that government has not taken into consideration some of the recommendations industry put on the table on several issues, specifically relating to the financial aspects of the regulations. For example, there is no clarity around how mining companies can withdraw their provisioned funds once they are ready to begin closure and rehabilitation. The biggest concern for the mining industry is the inclusion of financial closure provisioning in the regulations, because of the magnitude of operations the total liability results in a significant amount of money that could have been used elsewhere.
• Mining companies find it challenging to put money aside in alignment with the current regulatory requirements, and often find themselves not provisioning sufficiently for closure.
As a result, mining companies end up on-selling the mine because the closure liability is too high.
• Participants highlighted that there is no alignment between the mining companies, governmental departments, and the South African Revenue Service on the current regulations.

• Several participants described the existing confusion around definitions and terminology used in the Financial Provisioning Regulations. The most often mentioned example related to the definitions used in the regulations for latent and residual risks. Evidently, the regulations require some work and government needs to engage with and incorporate comments received from industry.

• During the interview process, concerns were also raised around the practical implementation of the Financial Provisioning Regulations, specifically the operational application of the methodology in the regulations. For example, the requirement for an annual, concurrent, and final rehabilitation plan is not clearly understood, resulting in unnecessary action, documentation, and expenses for mining companies. Further, concern was raised about the lack of guidance on how the mining company needs to do things (For example, what should their studies look like to determine latent impacts, and how do they fund these studies?). Some participants highlighted that it is becoming so costly just to get the studies done, that it has merely become a 'grudge' buy for companies to try and comply.

• Several concerns were raised about the fact that the regulations keep changing, but it is not the significant or important aspects that change. Mining companies want to know that what they are being forced to do will be for the good of the mine, communities, and the environment. In other words, the regulations are not standardising what matters. This was articulated by participant 008: "What are the regulations really trying to achieve?" Unless these challenges are addressed, it will remain difficult to incorporate additional requirements such as climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. However, to ensure sustainable and lasting closure, it is clear that the regulations must be updated in line with industry recommendations and in consultation with impacted stakeholders.

Several participants highlighted that, traditionally, mining regulations in South Africa have excluded people from consideration during closure and rehabilitation planning. However, with the new Financial Provisioning Regulations, there is a growing focus on the social aspects of closure and social impacts beyond closure. One participant clarified that the consensus between regulators and mining companies to simply plant grass on a mine site is inadequate in addressing the rehabilitation of the operational impacts. Mining companies cannot expect to uplift communities and build socialecological resilience by planting grass and trying to revert the land back to how it was 30 years prior to operations. As highlighted by the Centre for Environmental Rights 2 , communities impacted by mining frequently shoulder the burdens of social, environmental, and economic challenges both during the mining operations and in the aftermath of mine closure (Sefatsa & Horsfield, 2022). As a result, regulations are now factoring in the social consequences of closure and acknowledging the significance of an enduring and sustainable final state that encompasses feasible and lasting land uses for neighboring communities.

Despite the growing focus on the social aspects of mine closure in South Africa's closure regulations, planting grass for grazing remains a popular method of rehabilitation amongst mining companies, as highlighted by several participants. The underlying notion for this activity is to rehabilitate the land to its "pre-mined" state, which it seems in many cases was grazing. This method of rehabilitation it seems is also underpinned by the current regulations as highlighted by the following statement extracted from Impala Platinum's ESG Report (2021:57): "Although we have a statutory obligation to restore grazing as a minimum, we are constantly reviewing and aligning our post closure land use with the demands and requirements of the landowners." However, I believe mines should start looking beyond this notion and start thinking of how they can rehabilitate the land for new purposes and ways that can uplift a community and build resilience to climate change impacts. Rehabilitation should focus on how the mined land can be improved upon for now and the future. As such, I think it is important for this idea to be incorporated into the regulations, in order to drive sustainable mine closure. Although the new regulations place an increased emphasis on the social side of closure, some participants believe that the regulations over rely on agriculture as a post-mining economy, which is not always feasible. According to several participants, regenerative practices may provide better longterm results, but must be aligned with sustainable post-mining land uses.

Evidently, best practice guidelines, regulatory requirements, and standards are driving listed companies to integrate closure more comprehensively in their businesses, albeit slowly. The more the regulations improve, the more you force companies to think about closure, driving mining companies to review their systems to align to the regulations or the guidelines they have signed up to. As participant 001 explained: "Closure is currently just a tick-box exercise." This sentiment was echoed by several participants including participant 002 who said, "Some mines are trying, other are just tick-boxing." It is because of this that the mining industry needs to rapidly shift to more integrated, progressive closure and rehabilitation practices, which can be enormously beneficial for the mine, as well as the environment and surrounding communities. Progressively working on closure allows the mining company to see where the issues are upfront and then rectify these issues over the longer term, thereby avoiding the last-minute scramble or "emergency" response to achieve closure.
Consequently, the regulations play a fundamental role in driving this change and achieving sustainable closure.

div.head: The Rise in Integrated Closure Planning
div.p: A key aspect of my findings was the emergence of the idea of integrated closure planning. Integrated closure planning, according to several participants, refers to the process of planning for closure even before exploration begins. According to participants, with climate change and tailings breaches, the industry is starting to look more closely at closure plans. As per best practice described in Anglo American's Mine Closure Toolbox (2019:4), a key element of integrated closure planning is defining your "post-closure vision upfront to ensure that the mine is designed and operated in a manner that is geared towards closure." This statement, for me, is really the crux of integrated closure planning, as highlighted by the subsequent findings. Many of the participants explained that mine closure planning should be integrated and included right from the pre-feasibility phase and should influence or shape how the mine is subsequently constructed. According to the literature, in order to mitigate the socialecological challenges associated with mining operations, it is important for mine closure and rehabilitation to be thought of as a long-term, integrated planning process, rather than as an end-oflife procedure (Mpanza et al., 2021). The notion of integrated closure planning was highlighted by several participants. For example, participant 001 very clearly stated that "Closure should start at exploration." This statement was further supported by participant 005, who explained that "you really should be thinking about closure more or less as you get started." Several more participants emphasized the importance of integrated closure planning, including participant 006, who acknowledged that "if we plan for closure right up front as much as we possibly can, that will help the mining company in the end."

The main benefits of integrated closure planning for the mining company are related to cost benefits, this is because integrated closure planning ensures that costs that would usually pop up later on are avoided right up front. This is supported by best practice detailed in the ICMM's Closure Best Practice Guide (2019:10): "Early consideration of mine closure will make it easier and more cost effective to achieve final closure objectives and can improve the opportunities for relinquishment."

However, in order to realize these benefits, the ICMM highlights that mining companies need to design for mine closure from the earliest stages of exploration and mine development. A closure risk assessment at exploration identifies aspects of operations that could lead to risks later. As such, designing operations for these risks up front means that mining companies can save a lot of money.

Additionally, according to the literature, integrated closure planning can enhance the efficacy of mine closure plans and ensures that all possible outcomes have been thought of and included. Although many of the participants were in support of integrated mine closure planning because of the cost benefits associated with this practice, they also suggested that integrated closure planning can have a positive impact on communities and the surrounding environment.

As such, integrated closure planning should, alongside the economic factors, also take into consideration social and environmental factors from the early stages of exploration and continue to do so throughout the mine's life cycle. Signatories to the World Gold Council's Responsible Gold Mining Principles (2019:08), for example, need to recognise the important of integrated land use planning and "give meaningful consideration to the land access needs of nearby communities and to the preservation of biodiversity." This is because the environment and community are inextricably interlinked, in other words one cannot function optimally without the other. Participant 003, for example, highlighted the fact that "the moment you start drilling, you can already determine some of these (environmental and social) things." Recognising the importance of a sustainable post-closure land use, it is important to incorporate this consideration during the pre-feasibility and licensing phases. To implement effective and sustainable closure, it becomes crucial to establish and outline land utilisation post-mining during the pre-feasibility stage, including plans for economic diversification as well.

According to several participants, it is also important to consider what is realistically viable on the ground compared to what has been committed in the closure plans at the pre-feasibility phase. To achieve this, participant 001 believes that "…closure should change to a more integrated, technical field in mining, where it is very cross-functional and transvers in the departments that work on it."

During my review of company reports, I found that several companies are starting to refer to integrated closure planning. For example, in Impala Platinum's ESG Report (2021:56) they stated that their closure and rehabilitation strategy "focuses on ensuring a sustainable post-mining legacy from the project planning phase onwards." Further, the same report stated that Impala Platinum (2021:56) "strives to entrench the concept of "design for closure" across our operations by ensuring that all aspects of rehabilitation are defined at the project planning phase." Similarly, Anglo American stated in their Sustainability Report (2021:45) that they take a "cradle-to-cradle approach by beginning to plan for closure in the exploration phase, and continuing until a sustainable post-mining land use and legacy has been achieved." Interestingly, I also found reference to integrated closure planning in Exxaro Resources ESG Report (2021:38): "We actively plan our operations with closure in mind, ensuring adequate financial resources are available to meet our rehabilitation commitments."

In line with this review of company reports, I also tried to see if I could identify any examples of mining companies currently incorporating climate change adaptation in mine closure and rehabilitation planning. I also extracted the following statement from Anglo American's Sustainability Report (2021:45) "Our principal climate-related risk is the potential impact of physical climate change on water security for our organisation and host communities." Several participants explained that mining requires enormous amounts of water, without which operations will cease. One participant described their plan to ensure continued water access despite the potential impact climate change may have on water availability. They want to reduce their dependence on the local water catchment area by producing their own potable water.

They went on to explain that by doing this they "leave" more water in the catchment area for other water users, such as the local communities. Whilst most companies are concerned about access to water from an operational perspective, some companies are also concerned about the communities' access to water. Participant 005, for example, described how water scarcity is impacting communities in their vicinity. Firstly, wells in the area are drying up, particularly during the dry, summer months, and secondly, subsistence farmers are noting that rains have become unpredictable, resulting in increased periods of dryness and less water availability. On the other hand, participant 008 merely described the devastating effect of water scarcity on operations. When asked about the impact of water scarcity on the community, participant 008 responded by saying: "We haven't really quantified the impacts of water scarcity on the communities."

Based on these findings, it is clear that there is a need for climate change adaptation in the mining industry, specifically given the impacts of climate change on water availability and the industry's heavy reliance on water from an operational perspective. As such, the following section unpacks how climate change adaptation could be incorporated into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa.

div.head: Incorporating Climate Change Adaptation in Mine Closure and Rehabilitation
Strategies
div.p: In this section, I use my findings to explore how climate change adaptation practices could be incorporated into closure and rehabilitation planning in South Africa. When asked about incorporating climate change adaptation in closure planning, participants highlighted two important considerations. Firstly, the importance of progressive or concurrent rehabilitation and secondly, the value of effective stakeholder engagement.

div.head: Progressive or Concurrent Rehabilitation
div.p: According to several participants, progressive or concurrent rehabilitation is another concept that has grown in popularity across the mining industry. This was aptly expressed by participant 005 who explained that "the other thing that mining companies are realizing is that progressive rehabilitation is probably a better way than just planning for abrupt closure way down the line." Mining companies have realised that progressive rehabilitation is a better approach for lowering the burden of doing rehabilitation. In terms of the Financial Provisioning Regulations, the concept of 'annual' or 'concurrent' rehabilitation is now termed as 'progressive' rehabilitation, which is a term already understood by the mining industry and is the term I will use going forward. In essence, progressive rehabilitation pertains to the execution of closure activities throughout the operational phase.

Progressive rehabilitation on mining sites includes, for example, revegetation, sediment control, and drainage management. As explained by several participants, progressive rehabilitation activities typically begin with the restoration of soil, thus promoting the regeneration of, and consequently, the restoration of ecosystems post closure. One participant explained that progressive rehabilitation is the most effective mechanism to protect against risks associated with unplanned or unexpected closure. This is because the disturbed mining footprint left un-rehabilitated may be at an acceptable standard and is kept to a practicable minimum throughout the life of mine. This reduces the potential liability of the site from unplanned or unexpected closure.

Additionally, as is the case with integrated closure planning, progressive rehabilitation is a costeffective alternative to traditional rehabilitation, as well as the best way to reduce the mine's financial liability over the long-term. Several participants explained that progressive rehabilitation is the more cost-effective method of closure, because by the time operations cease, around 80% of the mine could already be rehabilitated, making it far easier and cheaper to rehabilitate the remaining 20% at the time that operations come to an end. In alignment with this finding, participant 002 explained that "concurrent rehabilitation is far more cost effective than accumulating large sums of money for closure." However, participants highlighted that to reduce your costs, the mining company needs to be implementing progressive rehabilitation throughout the process.

In other words, you need to design for closure in terms of progressive rehabilitation and how this will fit into your daily operations to ensure you do not hamper operations and daily operations do not destroy what you have rehabilitated. Anglo American's Mine Closure Toolbox (2019:42) provided further context by explaining that "Another key component of managing closure liabilities is to ensure that concurrent rehabilitation opportunities are optimized throughout the life of the operation to decrease liability, test sustainable rehabilitation prescriptions, build stakeholder confidence and assist with managing other environmental impacts."

The rise in popularity of progressive rehabilitation was also reflected in the review of mining company reports. For example, in Impala Platinum's ESG Report (2021:56) I found the following statement related to progressive rehabilitation: "through effective closure planning and concurrent rehabilitation, we strive for our mines to leave a positive, healthy and sustainable legacy." They went on to explain that all their tailings storage facilities have commenced with progressive rehabilitation, including revegetation, dust management, and water management. According to their report, progressive rehabilitation activities are "a cornerstone of our efforts to reduce the loss of biodiversity, habitat and ecosystem disturbance." I also found reference to progressive rehabilitation efforts in Anglo American's Sustainability Report (2021:27): "we require operations to develop and implement five-year rehabilitation plans that outline targets, monitoring, maintenance and management programmes to drive towards relinquishment." Although many mining companies mention progressive rehabilitation, my findings suggest that these companies fail to describe the methodology for implementing progressive rehabilitation. One participant echoed this concern and suggested that the solution would be to push the cost reduction aspect of progressive rehabilitation to get mining companies to adopt progressive rehabilitation more aggressively.

Whether mining companies implement progressive rehabilitation or traditional rehabilitation, the main aim of rehabilitation is to achieve physical and geochemical stability of the mine site. As explained by participant 003, rehabilitation refers to the process of "reinstating some sort of ecosystem that is self-perpetuating in terms of vegetation." This sentiment is supported by the literature, which explains that, ultimately, rehabilitation activities aim to reinstate fully functioning ecosystems and restore land productivity. When considering rehabilitation, mining companies need to ask themselves what the purpose and end goal of the rehabilitation activity is. Across the mining industry, closure happens by domain. When a project is initiated, the mining company needs to conduct a feasibility study and environmental and social impact assessments. Mining companies need to provide conceptual closure plans in these reports. Each mine then identifies a list of domains during the conceptual closure plan phase to which they must assign closure options.

Everything constructed by the mine must be thought about and provided for from a closure perspective in the mine's closure plan. When they are ready to close a domain, there is a list of activities that they need to complete to reach physical and geochemical closure. Thereafter, the mining company decides on the final usage of the land, and that is usually when stakeholder engagements come into play. According to participant 007, once a mining company has secured the various domains, they start engaging with doorstep communities in terms of what the community wants with each domain post-closure. However, a mining company will only consider an option suggested by the community if that option is economically viable for the mine. Participant 007 further explained that the mining company will also consider the following when deciding on closure options:
1. What area are we operating in?
2. What does the community use the surrounding land for currently?
3. What benefit is there for the land/environment and the community from the proposed activity?
For each domain, the mining company must decide on what to leave behind. These decisions will lead to a list of closure and rehabilitation activities that will be implemented for each domain on site.

As explained by participant 007, post-closure, the different rehabilitated areas (domains) of the mine should be compatible with the surrounding landscape, to support spatial continuity of land use and protection of local critical habitat. Currently, most rehabilitation activities are focused on growing vegetation, and trying to find plants that will adapt and grow well within the environments in which they are planted.
Typically, the following domains are present on a mine site, as described by participant 007:
1. Pits -which refer to an opening created by the extraction of the ore.
2. Waste dumps created through extraction, because not every material extracted contains valuable minerals.

3. Tailings Management Facility -the outcome of the material you treat is the tailings (for example, gold mining companies typically only process 1 gram of gold per ton of material extracted, the rest of the material goes to the tailings facility).
4. The plant, which processes the materials that come out of the pit (requires decontamination).
5. Supportive infrastructure -buildings, etc. (easy to dismantle).
6. Water infrastructure, such as dams, settling ponds and run-off water management systems.
7. Roads and other disturbed areas -roads are usually left behind because communities want to use them.
8. Underground mining -ventilation, lifts, equipment, etc.

According to the literature (Morrison-Saunders et al., 2016;Watson and Olalde 2019;Doley & Audet, 2013), and supported by several participants interviewed in this study, the rehabilitation of these domains should achieve three key objectives:
• The long-term stability and sustainability of land use, soil and water quality and availability.
In addition, the post-closure mine landscape is compatible, wherever practicable, with the surrounding landscape.

• The partial or full repair of ecosystem functionality to reinstate biodiversity, as well as provide ecosystem services for local communities, as well as animals. Where applicable, rehabilitation of disturbed areas that support or enhance the protection of critical habitat and protected species.
• The prevention of pollution of the surrounding communities and environments, ensuring that residual environmental impacts are reduced to acceptable levels post-closure.

Throughout the interview process, participants made it clear that land that has been fundamentally altered by mining activities cannot be restored to pre-mining conditions, nor can you achieve the complete restoration of historical ecosystems. Participants suggested a range of alternative rehabilitation solutions which focused on the use of a combination of alternative species to rehabilitate the land to a usable, sustainable post-mining state. According to participants, to ensure successful rehabilitation it is crucial to bring the responsibility of closure to the right departments, because mine closure requires technical expertise, as well as environmental expertise. According to participant 005, post closure land use considerations are driven by "the operational mine footprint, local communities and value biophysical components of the landscape." The most challenging domain to rehabilitate are the tailings storage facilities, as these domains require discussions with the community to determine what is feasible. For example, if the community wants to plant crops on the tailing's storage facility after closure, then the mine needs to make sure that the soil isn't contaminated, the walls of the facility need to be stabilized and all water on the surface of the facility needs to be removed. The importance of effective stakeholder engagement and the role it plays in successful rehabilitation and mine closure is discussed in the subsequent section.

div.head: The Value of Stakeholder Engagement
div.p: Throughout the interview process, all participants mentioned the critical role local communities play in closure and rehabilitation planning.

For example, participant 002 explained how "…an important part of your mine closure plan, aside from environmental obligations, is looking at what happens to those towns and those communities post-mining and can they be sustainable, and if so, how?" This opinion was supported by participant 001, who clearly stated that "It (mine closure) is all about engagement." Currently, there is a big push in industry for closure plans to integrate the social aspects of closure and rehabilitation more comprehensively, whereas before closure was largely focused on the environmental and technical aspects. When asked about the social aspects of closure, participant 008 explained "there is a lot more focus on our social aspects, obviously." This is further illustrated in best practice guidelines such as the ICMM's Integrated Mine Closure Guide (2019), which consists of quite a strong social component. Community engagement is key to successful closure planning because the community may not want the land restored to pre-mining conditions. Often, communities want the mining infrastructure and facilities instead of having them broken down and restoring the disturbed area to virgin land. Consequently, it is important to establish and consider what the community wants with the land. Stakeholder engagements are often facilitated through community forums, which help mining companies and communities formulate various viable options. In these sessions, the mining company considers how they can repurpose some of the infrastructure or facilities on site for use by the community. In most instances in South Africa, agriculture is considered the first prize. However, participants also highlighted several alternative community requests during closure engagements, such as jobs, local procurement, income generating activities, hospitals, maternity wards, and schools. Several participants also went on to explain that engaging with doorstep communities early on can ensure the long-term success of your rehabilitation activities. This was echoed in the literature by Stevens (2021), who explained that to ensure productive and safe post-mining land use and thriving communities, local governments and mining companies should ensure that community members are actively and equally involved in closure discussions, right from the planning phase all the way through to post-closure monitoring. Additionally, participant 002 highlighted that by "Partnering with communities early on, they can help you identify solutions that make them more resilient." Communities possess the local knowledge relating to biodiversity, ecosystems, and cultural heritage in the area. As such, communities can acknowledge and identify their vulnerabilities and then, working with the community, mining companies are able to identify viable rehabilitation and closure solutions. Interestingly, the literature also recommends the mining industry seizes the opportunity presented by climate change to collaborate with communities, governments, and other impacted stakeholders in adapting to climate change impacts. This recommendation was support by participant 002 who explained that "Partnering with the communities can build resilience to climate change impacts."

According to the literature, an effective mine closure plan should enable communities to achieve an improved, or at least sustained, quality of life after the mine has ceased operations. This was reflected in several of the company reports I reviewed as part of the data collection process. For example, in Impala Platinum's ESG Report (2021:100), Impala stated that "Our social interventions are designed as far as possible to address these issues, and to enable host communities and economies to thrive well beyond the closure of our mines." To achieve this commitment, the Impala (2021:100) goes on to explain that they "identify community projects based on a needs analysis, undertaken in consultation with stakeholder representatives from communities, local government, and employees".

Similarly, Anglo American explained in their Sustainability Report (2021:05) that "as a responsible mining company, we have a role in supporting host communities to thrive through and beyond this (closure) change." They also expanded on this statement by clarifying that they are "committed to delivering a lasting, positive contribution to our host communities, beyond the life of our mines."

Again, the mining company highlighted that this comes down to understanding and responding to community needs and priorities. Lastly, Sibanye Stillwater's IAR (2021:214) reflected similar statements. For example, they state that their aim is to "ensure that host communities can sustain themselves post-mining." Their approach to accomplishing this involves partnering and cooperating with local government and additional stakeholders to advance alternative economic initiatives.

Several participants highlighted that an important component of community engagement is enabling the community. As an example, in situations where a feasible economic strategy for closure has been established, the authorised mine closure plan must explicitly outline the ownership of the alternative economic activities incorporated. This stems from the significance of community ownership in sustainable economic activities after mine closure. The concept of attaining a sustainable end-state should go beyond solely training community members and laid-off mine workers to adjust and participate in the newly established alternative economies. It should also empower them to take ownership of these economies. I identified an example of this in practice through the report review process. In Sibanye Stillwater's IAR (2021:220) they explained that although it is sometimes more convenient to contract a big company to assist with rehabilitation, an opportunity exists to "empower local communities", by allowing them to take control of rehabilitation activities, particularly since they are the very people who will need to sustain themselves in these areas once mine operations have ended. By using the local community to assist with rehabilitation, the mining company is upskilling and diversifying the communities' abilities.
When asked about enabling communities post-closure, participants recommended the following:
• In terms of service delivery, it is important to try and implement as many infrastructure projects as possible, but projects that are self-sustaining (For example, solar-powered boreholes).

• In terms of your workforce and community at large, try to drive skills development programmes, but in a wide variety of portable skills (For example, IT trades and computer skills). Furthermore, aid host communities in acquiring alternative skills for application in commercial endeavors and post-mine closure infrastructure utilisation.

• Importantly, focus on enterprise and supply chain development (i.e., setting-up businesses or supporting existing businesses to grow and develop so that they can tender for work or provide services to the mine and society at large).
• Teach people the value of working with money and saving for the future.
• Invest in the education of surrounding communities, so that schools are properly equipped.

Education is the way to break the cycle of poverty. Further, train employees to implement and manage mine closure plans. Lastly, encourage environmental education, for example planting fruit trees, pruning trees, waste management, and recycling.

• Develop and implement environmental programmes, whereby mining companies partner with communities on monitoring certain areas/sections within the mining area and baselines data at communal points. Environmental monitoring post-closure can be managed by the community over the long-term.
• Implement livelihood restoration plans whereby livelihoods impacted by mining operations are restored to, a minimum, the level it was before the project arrived and, if possible, better.

Hand-in-hand with enabling communities post-closure, is preparing communities for closure. As participant 005 put it: "you don't want to create unnecessary fear. You don't want to create unnecessary expectations, so it is important to maintain open communication and consultation."

Several participants highlighted the importance of treading carefully when communicating with the community about closure. Participant 001 explained the importance of "prepping people that closure isn't bad, because as soon as you talk closure, they think they are going to lose their jobs." It was suggested that you start telling the community as early as possible that the mine will close one day, and then communicate with them on how you might assist them through upskilling, supporting small businesses, supporting entrepreneurs, diversifying economies, and helping the community to become self-sustaining (for example, through community gardens, tree planting, livestock, etc.). Engage your community from the pre-feasibility phase by facilitating community workshops that focus on what the community would like to achieve leading up to and post-closure. All impacted stakeholders, from the mining company to the local community, need to think about a way to promote economic activities post-closure to ensure a sustainable livelihood for communities once the mine closes its doors. Participant 004 explained that they (the community) "need to continue with a similar lifestyle post-mining, and they believe the mine is responsible to ensure that that happens." Evidently, the earlier the mining company engages with the community, the better for both the mining company, as well as the community.

div.head: Strengthening Social-Ecological Resilience to Climate Change Impacts
div.p: This section begins by exploring why there is a need to strengthen the social-ecological resilience of The climate crisis, particularly pronounced in Africa, has significant ramifications for the food and water security of both mining operations and nearby communities. This issue was highlighted in Exxaro Resources ' ESG Report (2021:17), which stated that "The changing climate will present significant challenges for water security in our operations and communities." Moreover, climate change accelerates the depletion of vulnerable ecosystems and farmland. This includes cultivated areas where post-rehabilitation maize yields fail to reach the levels achieved before mining activities.
During the interview process, participants highlighted the following risks relating to climate change:
• They are seeing a rise in temperatures and described how it has become hotter and drier in some locations.

• Several participants commented on the intensity of rainfall over the past several months and recorded more rain in some regions than previous years. Intense periods of heavy rainfall have caused flash flooding, impacting both the mine's operations, as well as surrounding communities. One participant described how one of their sites experienced such bad flooding that the surrounding community lost their crops.
• Participants were particularly concerned about the impact of rising temperatures on underground equipment functioning (for example, the ventilation systems).

• Many participants mentioned how doorstep communities are seeing and feeling a change (particularly the farmers, who are struggling to cultivate their crops). For example, subsistence farmers are noticing that rains have become unpredictable, increased dryness followed by severe flooding, wells are drying up and soil is becoming infertile.
• Most concerningly, from an operational and community perspective, is water availability in certain regions across South Africa.
• Lastly, participants described the significant safety risk to employees, as well as doorstep communities of increasing temperatures caused by climate change.

Related to these risks, participant 001 posed an important question: "How do we react now to reduce the risk in the future?" One suggested solution was conducting climate risk assessments as part of the closure planning process. A climate risk assessment, for example, would be used to understand rainfall patterns in 40 years' time, which will determine the closure and rehabilitation approach the mine will need to adopt in the short term. Understanding that the landscape might change over the long-term (from bush to desert, for example), will assist in determining what the mining company needs to start doing now already, so that when they get to scheduled closure, they are prepared for whatever may have happened to the landscape because of climate change. In other words, a climate risk assessment will determine how the mine rehabilitates at the time of closure.

Through a climate risk assessment, mining companies would be able to map or model different climate pathways, and ultimately identify climate adaptation pathways over the long-term. Interestingly, participant 001 highlighted that "Climate adaptation pathways are quite easy to implement if you get the necessary buy-in and understanding." In this way, mining companies can integrate climate studies with their closure plans and rehabilitation activities. Further, my findings suggest that to understand how the changing climate may affect mine closure plans and rehabilitation, mining companies could use internationally recognized climate projection models that correspond to the closure period. Additionally, one participant mentioned running long-term trials on areas that have already commenced with rehabilitation to see how the rehabilitation mix reacts to changes in rainfall and temperature patterns over the long-term. The point is then to accordingly adapt your rehabilitation mix over the years leading up to closure. For example, the mine commits to reinstate the mined area to arable land, and the land has a potential to produce five tonnes of crop under current climate conditions. However, climate change predictions indicate that rainfall will reduce by the time the mine is scheduled for closure. This means the crop production prediction of five tonnes will need to be adjusted to, say, only three tonnes. It is the responsibility of the mining company then to advise the community on this and help them to start thinking about other, more drought-resilient crops, for example. Importantly, participant 003 highlighted that mining companies "need the flexibility to be able to adapt, in other words flexibility to go either way, whether its cooling or going hotter, if it's raining more or less, both sides need to be addressed because we do see variability." As mentioned in previous sections, to ensure closure success however, planning for how this will be achieved should be done before commencing with mining operations. Several participants made it clear that climate change adaptation is already being considered more and more in the mining industry when planning for closure and rehabilitation. Further, signatories to the World Gold Mining Council Principles (2019:08) need to ensure that their "long-term closure strategy doesn't impact the host community" and they need to "include climate change in closure strategies". On the other hand, participant 005 highlighted that "assessing what is going to happen down the line and how climate change will affect mining infrastructure and the environment and how that would, therefore, impact closure has not been assessed. So that's going to get people thinking." One participant suggested that the uptake in climate change adaptation is mostly being done by the bigger, listed companies who are serious about climate change reporting because they are listed on stock exchanges that require climate change reporting as part of their environmental commitments. Junior mining companies, however, are not that inclined to consider climate change adaptation yet. • The community is still very much connected to the environment; hence, it is crucial to include the community in mine closure and rehabilitation discussions right from the pre-feasibility phase. Given the capacity of mining operations to disturb habitats through land disruption and pollution, the responsibility of mining companies to restore, monitor, and manage biodiversity remains an essential obligation. In this regard, NbS and EbA could play an important role in the restoration and management of impacted environments and habitats. For example, the development and implementation of natural wetlands on impacted land can assist with the regeneration of surrounding ecosystems, lending itself to increased ecosystem functioning and the sustained provision of ecosystem services to surrounding communities. This is particularly important in rural areas, as communities in these areas are still heavily reliant on the provision of ecosystem services, for example subsistence farmers, firewood, fruit picking, medicinal plants, water, etc.

• Several participants highlighted the importance of off-site initiatives from a NbS and EbA perspective, that are not necessarily related to mining and rehabilitation. For example, bee keeping. The aim is to try and positively impact the community by diversifying the area around you in terms of alternative skills post-closure. Another interesting initiative highlighted by one participant was the upskilling of members of the community or current employees to manage environmental monitoring during operations, as well as post closure.
• One participant mentioned the potential for revegetation by seeding and planting with local, native species and/or non-invasive species that provide local socio-economic benefits.

"Active planting" encourages strategic vegetation development that supports local biodiversity and provides economic benefits for surrounding communities. Importantly, an active community role in revegetation will result in greater success due to shared 'ownership' of outcomes. Post closure land use objectives may include the following: o Reforestation and habitat creation; o The re-purposing of project infrastructure for beneficial use by the community or other third parties; and o Mixed land use, potentially including but not limited to: diversified agro-pastoral activities; sustainable forestry or agro-forestry; aquaculture or reservoir fisheries (pisciculture); plant or animal sanctuary; and/or biodiversity reserve. For example, in South Africa, a few mines are starting to look at livestock farming during operational life of mine as part of concurrent rehabilitation solutions.

• One participant supported the idea of mixed closure methods, in other words using a combination of NbS and EbA together with more traditional rehabilitation activitiesfoot_4 . This participant made it clear that there is never a single solution for closure and rehabilitation, but that a combination of options is often the best solution.

• When planning for rehabilitation, design and implement a self-perpetuating system, in other words a system that can reseed or germinate itself. Additionally, consider a more diverse species mix to ensure resilience over the long-term. One participant mentioned that from a NbS and EbA perspective, mining companies could consider developing community-led nurseries, which results in a seed stock for the species you need for progressive rehabilitation.
The report review process also highlighted the following interesting NbS-and EbA-linked rehabilitation initiatives:

• Eco-tourism as an alternative option for rehabilitating old pits. Eco-tourism is a type of tourism that centers on visiting extraordinary and often endangered natural environments, with the purpose of contributing to conservation efforts and engaging in wildlife observation.

• The concept of a village ecosystem for horticulture is aimed at establishing self-sustaining, food-secure communities while enhancing their ability to withstand the effects of climate change. For example, smallholder irrigation schemes that support local livelihoods and upskill surrounding communities.

• Anglo American's Sustainability Report (2021:27) mentioned that they will "implement nature-based solutions on land we manage." This was the only mine of the four reviewed that mentioned nature-based solutions in their report. Interestingly, they have signed a three-year agreement with a consultant to explore how NbS can help them achieve "positive biodiversity outcomes and support carbon neutral goals."

• Interestingly, Exxaro Resources mentioned "ecosystem protection" in their ESG Report (2021:15) and their adaptation approach focuses on several NbS and EbA solutions, such as maintaining and restoring wetlands, preserving land, and collaborating with emerging farmers to advance the development of climate-smart agriculture. Moreover, they lease rehabilitated land to communities for farming purposes, offering coordinated support in soil and water management, as well as fundamental land management skills.

Although it is evident that several novel rehabilitation solutions are being adopted by mining companies, it is important to bear in mind that a potential solution must have both an economic and environmental benefit in order for it to be successful. Additionally, rehabilitation solutions are guaranteed uptake and support if they have the added value of a socio-economic benefit. As the literature explains, the concept of NbS is based on the idea that healthy, well-functioning ecosystems can support the provision of a diverse range of services that support societal well-being. determine what this could look like and how it could be adopted by mining companies across South Africa.

div.head: Benefits versus Challenges of Incorporating Climate Change Adaptation
div.p: This section of the findings chapter is focused on objective two of this research study: determining the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure plans in South Africa.

The data collected throughout this research process, highlighted the following benefits associated with incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies include:
• Incorporating adaptation measures in mine closure strategies could help mining companies reduce operational greenhouse gas emissions.
• Climate adaptation measures can assist with social closure.
• Adopting climate change adaptation measures could assist with rehabilitation options, specifically with resilient rehabilitation.
On the other hand, the following are challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies:
• Understanding and quantifying what climate change adaptation means within mine closure strategies.
• Climate change adaptation is very difficult to disclose if you do not fully understand or appreciate it.
• Mining companies often lack the necessary resources relating to climate change adaptation (most mining companies do not have a dedicated climate change team).

• The hierarchy of priorities for mining companies. For example, climate change will be a problem and then something like COVID happens or commodity prices change and there is a much bigger problem. Further, when there are competing interests for resources, climate change is often the first issue to drop off the agenda. This was clearly articulated by participant 002: "…even if you embed those things (climate change) within your culture, if there's a crunch you will ultimately revert to those things higher up on your list." The issues higher on the list are usually related to social aspects involving employees and surrounding communities. It was evident that mining companies put people before the environment, even though one has an impact on the other. As participant 002 explained: "If your resources were limited, you would first address the community needs before you move to the climate stuff."

div.head: Chapter Summary
div.p: In summary, the findings suggest that there are many challenges to effective, sustainable closure in South Africa. Challenges include limitations in the legislation, a lack of resources, and even the mindset of the mining industry. Despite these challenges, the industry is seeing some positive shifts, particularly in the NbS approaches and the recognition that progressive rehabilitation is one way to reduce costs and ensure sustainable closure from a social perspective. Further, almost every participant I interviewed highlighted the need to engage with impacted stakeholders as early as possible, marking a positive change in the attitude towards surrounding communities. These shifts signal a transformative trajectory for mine closure, emphasizing both ecological preservation and responsible economic and social considerations. recommendations for further study. div.head: Limitations of the Study
div.p: Reflecting on the scope of this study reveals certain limitations that might influence the conclusions drawn. One noteworthy limitation lies in the focus on a specific subset of mines for interviews, as well as only interviewing sustainability experts employed by mining companies. This could potentially limit the perspectives gathered and omit the valuable insights of affected communities and government. However, this study aimed to be exploratory in nature, providing an initial understanding of certain complexities within the mining industry. Another limitation arises from the exclusive consideration of operational mines, without exploring those that have already closed. This focus might constrain the scope of insights gathered, excluding potential differences in challenges and practices between active and closed mines.

Additionally, the study's focus on the perceptions of participants and mine representatives only offers insights into subjective viewpoints. It is important to acknowledge that these perceptions might not fully represent the mining company they work for or communities surrounding the mines.

Furthermore, the practical actions taken by mining companies, which might contrast with their expressed intentions, also deserve consideration. Future research could unpack the alignment between what mining companies say in their reports compared to the practices that they implement.
In summary, while this study is not exempt from certain limitations, it serves as a stepping stone toward understanding the complexities of sustainability and climate change within the mining sector.

By acknowledging and addressing these limitations, the study remains relevant as a foundational exploration, providing insights into a space that merits deeper investigation and a more holistic perspective.

div.head: Concluding Remarks
div.p: As we traverse the evolving intricacies and growing seriousness of the impacts of climate change, it is more important than ever to consider what this means for more vulnerable communities and ecosystems in South Africa, such as those surrounding operational and abandoned mines across the country. Given that mines have a set lifespan and their closure is inevitable, it is important to consider how climate change may affect the mine from a social-ecological systems perspective at the time of closure and beyond. The presence of thousands of abandoned mines across South Africa (Watson & Olalde, 2019;Edwards & Maritz, 2019;Perkins et al., 2020) underscores the imminent environmental and social challenges that closure presents. Therefore, investigating current closure practices and finding ways to improve the process is crucial for ensuring sustainable and successful post-closure transitions. Given South Africa's firsthand experience of climate impacts, especially among vulnerable communities, integrating climate adaptation across sectors is urgent. Despite a growing focus on climate change adaptation in South African literature (Bai et al., 2018), a significant gap remains in addressing the vulnerability of rural and mining communities to projected climate impacts.
