the main objectives of this study. This research set out to explore the potential to strengthen the socialecological resilience of mining communities in the face of climate change impacts by incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa.This was enabled by unpacking the following three objectives (1) identify examples of mine closure strategies that already incorporate climate change adaptation thinking, (2) determine the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure plans, and (3) evaluate the extent to which incorporating climate change adaptation can strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts. The key findings are detailed below.Climate change adaptation thinking is not currently incorporated in mine closure and rehabilitationstrategies in South Africa. The first objective involved exploring the current mine closure and rehabilitation landscape in South Africa, in order to ascertain if there are any examples of mine closure strategies incorporating climate change adaptation. This involved a review of the current regulations governing mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa, a review of four mining companies' IAR or ESG/Sustainability reports, as well as semi-structured interviews with sustainability experts from mining companies. Through this review it was clear that when it comes to climate change, mining companies are mostly focused on climate change mitigation and resilience to climate change impacts from an operational perspective. Furthermore, although greatly improved from an environmental and social perspective, the current Financial Provisioning Regulations do not require mining companies to consider climate change impacts post-closure. As a result, the findings revealed that climate change adaptation is not currently considered a key aspect of mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. However, it is important to highlight that my review was limited, and did not explore the mining industry from a global perspective.Best practice guidelines significantly influence mine closure and rehabilitation activities. Exploring the current mine closure and rehabilitation landscape in South Africa further highlighted the significant influence of best practice guidelines on mine closure and rehabilitation activities. Best practice offers a roadmap for mining companies to navigate closure and rehabilitation, they serve as a reference point that mining companies can draw upon to ensure that their closure and rehabilitation strategies align with industry-accepted standards. My findings suggest that mining companies in South Africa rely heavily on best practice guidelines, such as the ICMM's Integrated Mine Closure: Good Practice Guide, the World Gold Council's Responsible Gold Mining Principles, and Anglo American's Mine Closure Toolbox to ensure a systematic and comprehensive approach to rehabilitation and achieving successful closure. However, the findings also highlighted that best practice disclosure norms are currently not challenging or changing industry practice sufficiently to achieve effective mine closure and rehabilitation.South Africa's mine closure regulations play a crucial role in guiding the change required in industry.As with any regulations, South Africa's Financial Provisioning Regulations play a crucial role in guiding and improving mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. Regulations make mining companies plan ahead for closure, which means they have to think about how to rehabilitate the impact they had on land, water, and air during operations. It also requires them to involve local communities in decisions about mine closure, thereby ensuring effective and sustainable closure.Regulations can encourage mining companies to come up with new and better ways to restore the environment after mining. The findings point to the role the regulations can play in encouraging the incorporation of climate change adaptation thinking into closure and rehabilitation strategies in order to strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mine communities to climate change impacts postclosure.Challenges outweigh benefits when incorporating climate change adaptation. The second objective of this study involved exploring the benefits and challenges of incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies. While incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies offers a multitude of benefits, encompassing environmental, social, and economic dimensions, the findings suggest that the challenges outweigh the benefits. Interestingly, the challenges were voiced by sustainability experts from mining companies in South Africa. Consequently, the practical motivation for mines to incorporate climate change adaption measures into their closure strategies appears rather minimal. It is evident that without external forces such as legislation or the collective influence of communities and legal bodies like the Centre for Environmental Rights, there might be little motivation for mining companies to proactively embrace climate change adaptation measures. However, an alternative approach could involve assisting mines in reframing their perception of climate change adaptation, aligning the advantages of adaptation with potential profits -a strategy closely aligned to the principles of ESG practices. This shift in perspective could serve as a catalyst for the integration of climate change adaptation measures into mine closure plans, bridging the gap between sustainability objectives and economic interests. By proactively addressing the challenges posed by climate change within the mining sector through the incorporation of climate change adaptation into closure and rehabilitation strategies, the mining sector can, hopefully, achieve more effective and sustainable closure.Stakeholder engagement is crucial when planning for closure and rehabilitation in South Africa.Objective three explored the extent to which incorporating climate change adaptation can strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts. The findings highlighted that a crucial part of strengthening social-ecological resilience is engaging with stakeholders when planning for closure and rehabilitation. Throughout the interview process, all participants mentioned the critical role local communities play in closure and rehabilitation planning.The findings found that engaging with surrounding communities early on can ensure the long-term success of rehabilitation activities. The overarching narrative that emerges from the findings reinforces the notion that stakeholder engagement, particularly with local communities, is not merely a procedural requirement but a strategic imperative. It contributes to the broader goals of sustainability by promoting holistic, adaptive, and contextually sensitive approaches to mine closure and rehabilitation. However, although regulatory progress has been made from an environmental perspective and the regulations now hold mine owners responsible for environmental liabilities, very little consideration is given to the negative social impacts of mine closure, as well as guidance for successful social transitioning post-closure.Progressive rehabilitation is fundamental for successful closure. Lastly, when considering objective three, the findings pointed to the importance of progressive rehabilitation for successful closure, and ultimately strengthening the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts post-closure. This contrasts starkly with older practices where rehabilitation was often postponed until the end of the mine's operational life. The research substantiates the transformative impact of progressive rehabilitation, as it enables the gradual recovery of the ecosystem, mitigation of environmental degradation, and the promotion of healthier and more sustainable landscapes well before actual closure. The underlying message from the findings extends beyond closure itself, highlighting the broader implications of progressive rehabilitation in strengthening social-ecological resilience within mining communities. Progressive rehabilitation efforts, when integrated with community engagement and support, contribute to the creation of resilient communities that are better equipped to withstand the challenges posed by climate change post-closure. In other words, progressive rehabilitation extends far beyond the life of a mining operation. Additionally, the positive impacts are not only confined to the immediate surroundings of the mine but ripple outward, fostering sustainable benefits for communities and ecosystems post-closure. In this section, I provide recommendations for incorporating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa. These recommendations were informed by the information I collected throughout the course of this research journey, and are aimed at strengthening the social-ecological resilience of mining communities post-closure. Plan for operations with closure in mind. To effectively integrate climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies, a proactive approach is essential. As such, I propose that mining companies incorporate closure and rehabilitation considerations right from the project's outset as part of closure best practice. By factoring in the eventual end of operations during initial planning stages, companies can seamlessly include climate change adaptation measures across various operational and social-ecological aspects. This involves aligning infrastructure design, waste management procedures, rehabilitation plans, and community engagement efforts with long-term, resilient closure objectives in mind. As highlighted by several participants, integrated closure planning is gaining increasing traction as a cost-effective alternative to traditional closure planning. As such, my recommendation is for mining companies to strategically integrate climate change adaptation measures into various facets of their operations and closure and rehabilitation plans as part of their integrated closure planning strategy. Expand the financial provisioning regulations. Expanding the Financial Provisioning Regulations is a vital step toward integrating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa. As a suggestion, a starting point would be to broaden the regulations to encompass consideration of the potential impacts of climate change on post-closure environments and communities. This could be achieved, for example, by including climate modelling as a regulatory requirement. This would ensure that mining companies consider projected climate impacts beyond the life-of-mine and factor these impacts into closure and rehabilitation planning. Furthermore, adequate financial provisioning should not only consider traditional closure costs but also factor in the long-term measures required to strengthen social-ecological resilience to climate impacts post-closure. This expansion would ensure that mining companies allocate sufficient funds for ongoing monitoring, adaptive management, and necessary interventions related to climateinduced challenges. Strengthening the Financial Provisioning Regulations in this manner could contribute to the lasting social-ecological resilience of mining communities beyond closure. Engage regularly with impacted stakeholders. Engaging regularly with impacted stakeholders is a crucial recommendation for effectively integrating climate change adaptation into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies in South Africa. As such, I suggest that mining companies facilitate discussions between both themselves and other impacted stakeholders, such as surrounding community members, to critically share perspectives and collaboratively work towards mutually beneficial post-closure objectives. Maintaining ongoing communication and collaboration with local communities, environmental experts, and relevant authorities ensures that climate adaptation measures remain contextually relevant and responsive to evolving climate dynamics, particularly as the mine nears operational end-of-life. Regular engagement fosters a shared understanding of climaterelated challenges and encourages the co-creation of solutions that align with the needs and aspirations of mining communities. By involving stakeholders throughout the closure and rehabilitation journey, mining companies can harness local knowledge, enhance adaptive capacity, and establish a foundation for sustainable, social-ecological resilience post-closure. Explore alternative adaptation responses. Most importantly, I suggest mining companies explore alternative adaptation responses within the mining industry. This involves considering a range of innovative and context-specific approaches beyond conventional adaptation solutions. For example, mining companies could investigate NbS that harness the inherent resilience of local ecosystems to combat climate impacts post-closure. For mine closures, this translates into actions like reforestation, wetland restoration, native vegetation propagation, and the establishment of green corridors. By mimicking natural processes and harnessing ecosystem services, NbS create multifaceted benefits that extend beyond immediate rehabilitation goals. These solutions enhance ecosystem functions such as water regulation, carbon sequestration, and soil stabilisation, which are instrumental in adapting to climatic changes. Further, these ecological services directly benefit local communities by reducing vulnerability to climate change impacts and ensuring sustained access to essential resources post-study, it became apparent that additional areas of investigation are necessary to enhance our understanding of climate change adaptation within the mining industry. Below, I describe three potential research fields for further study. Reducing the vulnerability of mining communities to climate change impacts. I propose further research into reducing the vulnerability of mining communities in South Africa to climate change impacts. Currently, much of the focus in the literature is on climate change adaptation and reducing the vulnerability of the urban poor to climate change impacts in South Africa (Bai et al., 2018). However, much less attention has been paid to reducing the vulnerability of rural communities, and specifically mining communities, to projected climate change impacts. Understanding the social dimensions of climate change adaptation in mining communities is crucial for effective closure and rehabilitation implementation. Further research could explore the socio-economic impacts of climateresilient closure and rehabilitation strategies on local communities. This might involve analysing how these strategies affect employment opportunities, livelihoods, and community well-being. Additionally, exploring the role of community engagement and participatory decision-making in shaping adaptation plans could provide insights into fostering greater community acceptance and support for sustainable mining practices.Economic implications and financial strategies. Through this process it has become apparent that the mining industry, like any industry, is fundamentally concerned about funds and the economic implications of their decisions. An example of this is the rise in integrated closure planning and progressive rehabilitation, which many participants highlighted because of its potential to reduce costs related to closure and rehabilitation. As such, a deeper examination of the economic implications of integrating climate change adaptation measures into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies is essential. Further studies could assess the cost-effectiveness of different adaptation options, including resilient rehabilitation approaches, such as NbS and EbA, and explore financial mechanisms that incentivise mining companies to adopt more sustainable practices when planning for closure and rehabilitation. This could involve evaluating the potential benefits of carbon pricing mechanisms, green bonds, and sustainable investment strategies, and how these financial tools can support the mining industry's transition towards climate resilience.Climate impacts on social-ecological systems after mine closure. Lastly, from the literature review it became evident that much of the literature on "climate change impacts on the mining industry" focuses on the climate risks mining operations currently face, with a lack of literature and research on the climate impacts after a mine closes. As such, understanding the link between climate change and social-ecological systems after mine closure is a crucial area deserving further study. From an environmental perspective, it is important to understand the interaction between climatic changes and the post-mining landscape. As these landscapes are in a state of recovery from mining activities, climate impacts such as shifting precipitation patterns, temperature changes, and hydrological shifts can greatly influence ecological restoration post-closure. As a result, further study into these dynamics can reveal valuable insights into boosting landscape resilience against climate pressures and ensuring sustainable closure. Recognising that climate change effects last beyond a mine's operational life requires further research into how climate trends influence ecological recovery, community adaptation, and long-term sustainability post-closure.

Using a NbS lens, this study investigated the role of nature-based and ecosystem-based adaptation in strengthening the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts postclosure. Adopting a NbS lens for this research aligns with the complexities of mine closure and climate change. Further, unlike conventional adaptation responses, nature-based solutions can address intertwined community-environment dynamics more effectively. As a result, this approach assisted in navigating the intricate relationships between social and ecological systems, advocating for innovative adaptation strategies for addressing climate change impacts post-closure. Amidst the challenges of reshaping institutions like mining companies, which tend to be resistant to change and where current change initiatives are hampered by profit-driven motives, I observed a growing shift towards more sustainable and long-lasting closure and rehabilitation processes. At the core of this reinforcing cycle were dedicated individuals within these mining companies who wholeheartedly supported the expanding movement towards positive change within the South African mining industry. Importantly, my findings uncovered three key aspects to adopting climate change adaptation in mine closure and rehabilitation strategies: (1) best practice guidelines significantly influence mine closure and rehabilitation activities; (2) the South African regulations governing mine closure play a crucial role in guiding the change required in industry; and (3) the mining industry must place an increased focus on the value of stakeholder engagements when planning for closure and rehabilitation. In conclusion, as the momentum for change builds and climate change impacts worsen, it is evident that collaborative efforts, regulatory alignment, and ethical considerations are required to propel the mining industry closer to a more sustainable and resilient future. div.head: Data Analysis
div.p: Qualitative data derived from interviews or documents typically consist of a large quantity of unstructured text, making this type of data difficult to analyse. Additionally, unlike quantitative data, there are no precise rules to follow when analysing qualitative data (Bryman et al., 2019). As per Preiser et al. (2022:270), the aim of qualitative data analysis is to unearth the "meaning" that emerges through various analysis methods. As I wanted to explore the nuance and diversity of perspectives across a variety of participants, qualitative methods of data analysis were ideal for exposing the diversity in perspectives I required for my research findings (Preiser et al., 2022). I utilised a qualitative coding technique to analyse the data obtained from semi-structured interviews.
Furthermore, I employed thematic analysis to examine the data collected from the review of mining reports and policy scoping, spanning a period of approximately four months.

div.head: Coding
div.p: Given that my main method of gathering data was qualitative interviews, I opted for thematic coding as my primary technique to analyse the collected information. Coding qualitative data to find common themes and concepts is a form of thematic analysis (Bryman et al., 2019). Briefly, coding is a popular starting point for most forms of qualitative data analysis (Bryman & Bell, 2014), and it is understood as the process of "selecting, focusing, simplifying, abstracting, and/or transforming the data that appear in the full corpus (body) of written-up field note and interview transcripts" (Miles et al., The second limitation pertained to the interview process and the participants I invited to partake in my study. should be interpreted with some caution, as they might not fully capture the diversity and nuances that a larger, more diverse participant pool would provide. However, my aim in this research was not to capture a representation of how all mining companies in South Africa operate, but to understand, in depth, the perceptions that key individuals from selected mining companies have experienced and understand mine closure practices within their particular contexts.

div.head: WHY DO WE INVITE YOU TO PARTICIPATE?

div.head: WHAT IS THIS RESEARCH PROJECT ABOUT?
div.p: This research project is about determining how to build social-ecological resilience to climate change impacts amongst mining communities post life of mine. Existing social-ecological vulnerabilities within mining communities in South Africa make mining communities particularly sensitive to projected climate change impacts. As such, it is crucial to ensure that the communities that rely on and live near the mine whilst it is active can continue to live a sustainable life once the mine closes. Thus, the aim of this research is to explore the potential to strengthen the social-ecological resilience of mining communities to climate change impacts by incorporating climate change adaptation thinking into mine closure and rehabilitation strategies.

div.p: Stellenbosch University https://scholar.sun.ac.za Any information you share with me during this study and that could possibly identify you as a participant will be protected. I will not identify you nor the company you work for in my research report or other related publications. The following steps will be taken to ensure your anonymity:

• Identifiable data, such as your contact details and signed consent form, will be stored in a separate folder on my private laptop and on my private OneDrive, which are password protected, to which only I will have access. This data will be deleted once my master's research is examined and completed. I will also ensure that this information is not linked to the data collected during the interview in any way. Signed consent forms will not be shared with anyone.

• Digital documents, such as voice recordings, transcribed interviews and digital notes will be stored on the cloud through my private password-protected OneDrive, with a backup of all digital documents related to my thesis stored on my private password-protected laptop. Only the transcripts or typed notes will be shared with my supervisor/co-supervisor, with anonymised information.

• When conducting the interview, the only indicators I will make note of will be non-identifying, such as the mining sector you work for and your job title. However, your name, as well as the name of the mining company at which you work will not be disclosed. This ensures that all information collected during the interview is deidentified immediately.

• Any hand-written notes pertaining to the interview will be stored in a safe place and typed up as soon as convenient to secure them digitally. Again, I will not make notes of any identifiable information.
• The data collected during this research process will not be stored for future use after the completion of this project.
• The data collected during this research process will not be shared with any collaborators or researchers (locally or internationally).

If permission is granted by you, all interviews will be voice-recorded and transcribed. You will have the opportunity to review the audio recording/transcripts if you wish to do so. You may suggest edits to the transcript if you feel this is necessary to adequately reflect your response given during the interview. Only I will have access to the audio recording, whilst only the transcripts or typed notes will be shared with my supervisor/co-supervisor, with anonymised information. All digital information will be erased once my master's research is examined and completed.
